Users would report agents not finding obvious information, but engineers couldn't determine whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. Adding full production tracing lets teams diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, teams monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures all without monitoring the contents of individual conversations to maintain user privacy.
questions.question: True or false: Production tracing monitors the contents of individual conversations to debug agent failures.

questions.lessonTitle: Deployment Strategy for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This creates a deployment challenge because whenever teams deploy updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. Well-meaning code changes could break existing agents if all agents are updated to the new version simultaneously. To avoid disrupting running agents, teams use rainbow deployments, which gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This ensures that agents in the middle of research tasks can complete their work without interruption.
questions.question: What deployment strategy is used to avoid disrupting running agents when updates are deployed?
choices: Canary deployments that test on 5% of traffic first
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions
Blue-green deployments that replace all agents simultaneously
Rolling deployments that restart each agent one at a time
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments keep both old and new versions running simultaneously and gradually shift traffic, which is essential for stateful agent systems that cannot afford interruptions.

questions.lessonContent: Together AI released the Together Embeddings endpoint on January 11, 2024. This endpoint offers 8 leading embedding models that include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context capabilities. These embedding models are designed to provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. The platform also offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models available in 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. Additionally, these models can be accessed at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: What is the name of the benchmark used to evaluate the Together Embeddings models that includes UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models?

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings endpoint provides access to powerful embedding models at very competitive prices. According to the release announcement, these models are priced up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms. This makes them accessible for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification tasks. The pricing advantage allows developers to build AI applications more cost-effectively while still achieving state-of-the-art performance in embedding tasks.
questions.question: Together Embeddings models are priced up to 4 times cheaper than other popular embedding platforms.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers M2-BERT retrieval models specifically designed for long context applications. These models come in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k, representing 2,000, 8,000, and 32,000 token context windows respectively. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically has an embedding dimension of 768, which is the size of the vector output. These long context models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while preserving more meaningful contexts.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension size for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model has an embedding dimension of 768, which is the size of the vector output produced by the model.

questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings using the Together Embeddings endpoint, the process involves several sequential steps. First, you read data from a file in JSONL format using functions that extract samples from the data file. Next, you generate embeddings for these text samples using the Together API's embeddings endpoint. Finally, you transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors using tSNE to reduce them to 2D for visualization. The complete workflow also includes plotting these transformed embeddings to visualize relationships between different data sources.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in visualizing embeddings with Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together. To configure the client, you need to import the OpenAI client, provide your Together API key, and set the base URL to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". This enables seamless migration without rewriting your existing application code. The client can then be used with the same methods as the standard OpenAI embeddings API.
questions.question: What is the base URL configuration required to make the OpenAI client work with Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonTitle: RAG Integration Options with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings supports integrations with popular frameworks and vector databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation systems. Specifically, the platform provides integration options for MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex. These integrations allow developers to connect Together's embedding capabilities with their preferred tools for vector storage and retrieval pipelines. The documentation provides deep-dive tutorials for implementing RAG with each of these technologies.
questions.question: True or False: Together Embeddings provides integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for building RAG applications.

questions.lessonTitle: M2-BERT Retrieval Model Context Length Options
questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models designed for different context length requirements. The M2-BERT retrieval models come in three variants based on their maximum context length: 2k, 8k, and 32k context options. These models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing you to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while preserving more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: Which of the following represents the available context length options for M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed with three context length options: 2k, 8k, and 32k, as explicitly stated in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: To use the Together Embeddings endpoint with OpenAI-compatible API, you first need to import the OpenAI client library. Then, you create a client instance by providing your API key and setting the base URL to the Together API endpoint. Finally, you define a function to generate embeddings for your text input. These three steps form the foundation of integrating with the Together Embeddings API.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up the OpenAI-compatible client for Together Embeddings?
choices: Set base URL to Together API

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides code for visualizing high-dimensional embedding vectors using t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding). Since embedding vectors have dimensions too large to visualize directly, t-SNE transforms them into lower-dimensional representations suitable for plotting. The transform_tSNE function accepts parameters including n_components and perplexity. In the main visualization script, the perplexity parameter is set to 15, which controls the balance between preserving local and global structure in the data. This value represents a common default for medium-sized datasets being reduced to 2D for visualization.
questions.question: What is the perplexity value used in the t-SNE transformation for visualizing Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Document Processing with M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: One significant advantage of M2-BERT retrieval models is their ability to handle long documents without requiring chunking. These models support context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens, allowing users to generate embeddings for entire long documents in one pass. This approach contains more meaningful contexts in the embeddings compared to splitting documents into many short chunks. The capability is particularly valuable for applications involving lengthy legal documents, research papers, or comprehensive reports where preserving full context is essential for accurate retrieval.
questions.question: True or False: M2-BERT retrieval models require documents to be split into many short chunks to generate embeddings.

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Data Source Relationships in Embedding Visualizations
questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings using t-SNE, the spatial relationships between different data sources reveal their semantic similarity. The code visualizes data from sources including arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl. According to the visualization results, texts from each data source are somewhat closely located within the embedding space. Specifically, github and stackexchange texts appear similar due to their technical programming nature, while book and c4 texts also show similarity. However, github and book texts are less related to each other in the embedding space.
questions.question: Which pair of data sources shows the GREATEST semantic similarity when visualized using Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that 'we can also see the similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are less related.' GitHub and StackExchange are both technical/programming sources, showing the greatest semantic similarity.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization workflow for embeddings involves three key sequential steps. First, you must define functions to extract samples from a data file, which involves reading JSONL format and handling context length limitations. Next, you generate embeddings using the Together API by calling the embeddings.create() method with your selected model. Finally, because embedding vectors are typically too high-dimensional to visualize directly (e.g., M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K has dimension 768), you apply tSNE transformation to reduce the embedding dimensions to 2D for plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct sequence for processing embeddings from extraction to visualization using the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering that builds upon a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. The developers selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model after evaluating several open-source alternatives including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04 trillion total parameter model with 32 billion active parameters. This Mixture-of-Experts design allows the model to efficiently route computations to specialized experts while maintaining strong overall performance across diverse coding tasks.
questions.question: What is the total number of parameters in the base model Kimi K2.5 used for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: The application of large language models to code generation has evolved significantly over time. Early applications typically focused on autocomplete applications, where the model predicts the next token or completes partial code snippets. Subsequently, instruction tuning transformed models into coding assistants capable of responding to user requests with full code solutions. In the last year, software engineering agents have achieved widespread adoption, pushing models beyond simple chat interactions to autonomously navigate repositories and solve complex engineering tasks. This progression represents a fundamental shift from reactive code completion to proactive problem-solving.
questions.question: Software engineering agents have achieved widespread adoption in the last year, pushing models beyond chat to autonomously navigate repositories and solve complex engineering tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 model is trained in two distinct phases to achieve frontier-level coding performance. The first phase is continued pretraining, which aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. The second phase involves large-scale reinforcement learning, which improves end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. These two phases work together to transform a general-purpose model into a specialized coding agent.
questions.question: What are the two training phases used to develop Composer 2?
questions.explanation: The document explicitly states that Composer 2 is trained in two phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends the Kimi K2.5 base model through a three-phase continued pretraining approach. The first and most computationally intensive phase trains at a 32k token sequence length. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension that increases the maximum sequence length to 256k tokens. The third and final phase is a brief supervised fine-tuning phase focused on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to progressively specialize its coding knowledge and capabilities before moving to reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the maximum sequence length used during the long-context extension phase of continued pretraining?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks that run in environments emulating real Cursor sessions. The problem distribution reflects the most common use cases in software engineering. According to Figure 3 in the technical report, the training distribution covers many aspects of software engineering absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. The categories include debugging, new feature development, refactoring, understanding codebase, documentation, testing, code review, optimization, devops, migration, and deletion. In later training stages, simple heuristics are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: RL training in Composer 2 uses a problem distribution that captures many software engineering aspects absent from popular AI coding benchmarks, including debugging, new feature development, refactoring, and code review.

questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, Composer 2 adds a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The penalty formula uses hyperparameters k and q which define the curvature, with the input x being a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls. This enables the model to learn particularly efficient behaviors such as making multiple tool calls in parallel.
questions.question: Which input components are combined to compute x in the nonlinear length penalty formula used in Composer 2's RL training?
choices: Thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns
Tool calling tokens and number of tool calls only
Only thinking tokens and final message tokens
Final message tokens and number of turns only
questions.explanation: The formula combines six components: thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. This weighted combination allows the penalty to reflect the total effort expended across the entire agent interaction.

questions.lessonContent: In Section 4 of the Composer 2 Technical Report, the reinforcement learning training process is described as a sequential pipeline. At a high level, RL training consists of first selecting a coding problem from the large set of training tasks, then generating multiple solution trajectories by having the agent attempt different approaches, and finally modifying the model parameters based on how well each solution performed. This creates a continuous improvement cycle where the model learns from its own generated solutions.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 which scored 44.2%, and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 which scored 38.0%. On public benchmarks, Composer 2 scores 73.7% on SWE-bench Multilingual and 61.7% on Terminal-Bench. CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team, which helps avoid train-set contamination that affects public benchmarks.
questions.question: What is the percentage score achieved by Composer 2 on CursorBench?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench tasks differ structurally from public evaluation benchmarks in two key ways. First, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Second, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: True or false: CursorBench tasks require fewer lines of code changes on average than public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale training, high availability, and independent scaling. These services include training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. The training stack uses Ray and PyTorch with a centralized reconciler that performs slot-based sample lifecycle state management, moving samples through a pipeline of distributed executors and implementing scheduling policies.
questions.question: How many regions did the Composer 2 production training job span for GPU compute?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute.

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation benchmark development process begins by identifying key dimensions of agent behavior that are important for real-world software engineering. These dimensions include intent evaluation (how the model handles ambiguous prompts), instruction-following evaluation, code quality evaluation, and interruption handling. Once these dimensions are identified, researchers select specific data points from actual coding sessions that can elicit these behaviors. Performance rubrics are then written to measure how well the model performs on each dimension. Finally, evaluation tasks are created to test the model on these rubrics, followed by running the model on tasks and computing accuracy metrics to assess performance.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the evaluation benchmark development process?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. There are several locations where you can place CLAUDE.md files: the root of your repo (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (files are pulled in on demand), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all sessions. You can name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git to share across sessions and with your team, or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: In which location can you place a CLAUDE.md file that will apply to all your Claude sessions across different projects?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code inherits your bash environment, giving it access to all your standard tools. While Claude knows common utilities like unix tools and gh, it won't know about your custom bash tools without explicit instructions. To make custom tools available to Claude, you must tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md. Without these steps, Claude cannot access or use your custom bash scripts and functions.
questions.question: Custom bash tools that you create in your shell environment are automatically available to Claude Code without any additional configuration.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (with the former recommended for team sharing), and use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions. Examples include adding Edit to always allow file edits, Bash(git commit:*) to allow git commits, or mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate to allow navigating with the Puppeteer MCP server.
questions.question: What are the four ways to manage Claude Code's allowed tools?
choices: Edit the .gitignore file, configure environment variables, modify the Claude config, or update the system PATH
Create a tools.md file, configure allowedTools in CLAUDE.md, edit .clauderc, or modify the model prompt
Use the /config command, edit claude.json, modify bash profile, or update MCP settings
Select "Always allow" when prompted, use /permissions command, manually edit settings.json, or use --allowedTools CLI flag
questions.explanation: The four documented ways to manage allowed tools are: 1) selecting "Always allow" during prompts, 2) using the /permissions command, 3) manually editing settings files, and 4) using the --allowedTools CLI flag.

questions.lessonContent: The explore-plan-code-commit workflow suits many problems and consists of four main steps. First, ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly tell it not to write any code. Second, ask Claude to make a plan for the specific problem, using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode which gives Claude additional computation time. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code. Fourth, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request. Steps one and two are crucial—without them, Claude tends to jump straight to coding a solution rather than researching and planning first.
questions.question: In the explore-plan-code-commit workflow, why is it important to explicitly tell Claude not to write code during the first two steps?
questions.answer: Because without explicit instructions not to code, Claude tends to jump straight to writing a solution rather than properly researching and planning first, which significantly reduces performance for problems requiring deeper thinking.

questions.lessonContent: Claude can effectively handle many git operations, with many Anthropic engineers using Claude for over 90% of their git interactions. Claude can search git history to answer questions about what changes went into specific versions, who owns particular features, or why an API was designed a particular way. Claude can also write commit messages by automatically looking at your changes and recent history to compose messages taking all relevant context into account. Additionally, Claude can handle complex git operations like reverting files, resolving rebase conflicts, and comparing and grafting patches.
questions.question: Claude can handle more than 90% of git interactions at Anthropic.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, connecting to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that specific directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file that makes servers available to anyone working in your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box. When working with MCP, using the --mcp-debug flag can help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: In which three locations can you configure MCP servers for use with Claude Code?
choices: ~/.claude directory, project root, and environment variables
Command line flags, .env files, and settings.json
Project config, global config, and .mcp.json file
Git hooks, npm scripts, and package.json
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config, in global config, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, use the -p flag with a prompt, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. It is important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each session. This mode allows Claude to power automations triggered by GitHub events, such as automatically inspecting new issues as they come in and assigning appropriate labels. Claude Code can also provide subjective code reviews beyond what traditional linting tools detect, identifying issues like typos, stale comments, and misleading function or variable names.
questions.question: What flag must be used to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Instead of supervising Claude, you can use claude --dangerously-skip-permissions to bypass all permission checks and let Claude work uninterrupted until completion. This works well for workflows like fixing lint errors or generating boilerplate code. However, letting Claude run arbitrary commands is risky and can result in data loss, system corruption, or even data exfiltration via prompt injection attacks. To minimize these risks when using --dangerously-skip-permissions, the documentation recommends using it in a container without internet access. There is a reference implementation using Docker Dev Containers that demonstrates this safe approach.
questions.question: The --dangerously-skip-permissions flag is safe to use in any environment because it only skips permission checks without any other risks.

questions.lessonContent: Some of the most powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. One approach is having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. Another technique used by Anthropic engineers is creating 3-4 git checkouts in separate folders, opening each folder in separate terminal tabs, and starting Claude in each folder with different tasks. Git worktrees offer a lighter-weight alternative by allowing you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task.
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using git worktrees over multiple git checkouts when running parallel Claude sessions?
choices: Git worktrees automatically sync changes between branches in real-time
Git worktrees require less disk space than multiple git checkouts
Git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog while providing isolated working directories
Git worktrees provide better performance for single-tasking scenarios
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, where each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. This makes option 0 correct.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together. Each color value ranges from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. For example, the color rgb(255, 147, 41) contains maximum red, moderate green, and low blue. An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage, resulting in approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single uncompressed image.
questions.question: What is the maximum value for each color channel (red, green, or blue) in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses a lossy compression technique that exploits how human vision works. Human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but tend to blur color together. This means you notice blurry edges but cannot detect slight color inaccuracies. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, then reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice. The image is divided into 8×8 pixel blocks and transformed into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges.
questions.question: JPEG reduces color resolution because human eyes resolve color with the same precision as brightness.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three main tricks to achieve lossless compression while preserving every pixel. The first trick is filtering or prediction, where instead of storing each pixel value directly, the compressor stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor (such as the pixel to the left or above). The second trick is LZ77, which finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with back-references to earlier occurrences within a 32 KB sliding window. The third trick is Huffman coding, which assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently. For example, a value appearing 60% of the time might get just 1 bit while rare values get longer codes.
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the three main tricks PNG uses for lossless compression?
questions.explanation: Filtering/prediction is one of PNG's three main tricks. It stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor rather than storing the actual pixel values. The other options (DCT transformation, run-length encoding, and wavelet coding) are not part of PNG's compression methods - DCT is used by JPEG for lossy compression, while PNG relies on filtering/prediction, LZ77 pattern matching, and Huffman coding.

questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression uses three key techniques in sequence to reduce file size while preserving all original pixels. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores only the differences rather than absolute values. After filtering, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references to earlier data. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values and longer codes to rare ones. This sequential pipeline transforms raw pixel data into a compressed PNG file.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG lossless compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: JPEG transforms pixel data from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color information. This conversion is essential because it allows JPEG to treat brightness and color differently during compression. The brightness component (luminance) carries most of the visual information humans perceive, while color (chrominance) contributes less to visual quality. By separating these components, JPEG can apply different compression strategies to each. This separation is what enables JPEG to exploit the human visual system's limitations effectively.
questions.question: To what format does JPEG convert pixels from RGB?
questions.answer: A format that separates brightness from color (luminance from chrominance)

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Size and Frequency Components
questions.lessonContent: JPEG processes images by dividing them into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforming each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs consist mostly of smooth gradients, most of the visual information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG exploits this characteristic by throwing away high-frequency details that humans won't notice, while preserving the smooth parts of the image.
questions.question: JPEG divides images into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details. True or false: JPEG throws away high-frequency details that humans won't notice.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: At high quality settings, JPEG compression produces results that are barely noticeable to the human eye. However, when compression is cranked up to higher levels, characteristic visual artifacts appear where fine details get lost. These artifacts manifest as visible blocking effects where the 8×8 pixel grid becomes apparent. The trade-off with JPEG compression is typically worth it: files become 10-20 times smaller with minimal visible difference to the original image at acceptable quality levels.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes JPEG compression artifacts at high compression levels?
choices: Blurring of all colors in the image
Blocking artifacts where fine details are lost
questions.explanation: At high compression levels, JPEG produces blocking artifacts where fine details are lost, making the 8×8 block structure visible. This is because JPEG throws away high-frequency details, and at extreme compression, the underlying block structure becomes apparent.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression involves converting the image into frequency components. First, the image is divided into 8x8 pixel blocks. Each block is then transformed to frequencies using a mathematical transform called DCT. Finally, the high frequency details that human eyes won't easily notice are quantized (reduced or eliminated), while preserving the important low-frequency smooth gradients.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG lossy compression?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering or prediction to compress images by storing differences between adjacent pixels rather than storing absolute values. The encoder examines each row and tries different prediction methods to find the one that compresses best. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub predicts from the left neighbor (best for horizontal gradients), Up predicts from the pixel above (best for vertical gradients), Average predicts from the average of left and above, and Paeth smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal based on which is closest.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method smartly picks between the left neighbor, the pixel above, or the diagonal pixel?

questions.lessonContent: After filtering, PNG uses the LZ77 algorithm to find repeated patterns in the data. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data and replaces any repeated sequence within that window with a back-reference pointing to the earlier occurrence. This tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the values directly. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size.
questions.question: True or false: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data to find and reference repeated patterns.

questions.lessonContent: PNG files organize compressed data into structured chunks, each with a specific purpose. The three required chunks are: IHDR (image header with metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual compressed image data), and IEND (end marker). Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint of the chunk's data. When you open a PNG, your computer recalculates this fingerprint to detect if the file has been corrupted.
questions.question: What type of checksum does PNG use to verify that data has not been corrupted?
questions.explanation: Each PNG chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint used to verify data integrity.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three main tricks in sequence to achieve lossless compression. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores the difference, which results in small numbers that compress well. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the filtered data and replaces them with back-references to earlier data. Third, Huffman encoding assigns shorter binary codes to more common values. Finally, the compressed data gets wrapped in the PNG file format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG's lossless compression algorithm (from prediction to final encoding)?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Two Periods of Roman Government
questions.lessonContent: There were two distinct periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire lasted from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Under the Roman Republic, Rome technically had an empire through its conquests. However, the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors instead of the earlier republican system of elected officials.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate honored him with the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' In 23 BCE, the Senate made Augustus consul for life, and he was also given the titles 'Princeps' (meaning 'first citizen,' which is the origin of the word 'prince'), 'Imperator' (meaning 'successful general,' which is the origin of the word 'emperor'), 'Pontifex Maximus' (meaning 'chief religious leader,' the origin of the word 'pontiff'), and the power to call the Senate, veto laws, and make laws.
questions.question: Octavian was granted the title 'Imperator' by the Senate after defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus attempted to reform public morals by promoting family life, though this was largely unsuccessful. He began the practice of declaring emperors gods and of picking their own successors, even calling Haley's Comet the spirit of Caesar. He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure, including roads, and encouraged the growth of business. Augustus established fire and police departments for Rome, created a strong money system, extended citizenship to more provincials, and famously said he 'found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble.'
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an accomplishment of Augustus?
choices: He established fire and police departments for Rome
He established the first Roman Senate
He extended citizenship to more provincials
He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure
questions.explanation: Augustus did not establish the first Roman Senate - the Senate existed since the Roman Republic. He did build infrastructure, extend citizenship, and establish fire and police departments.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name Augustus, meaning most high. Finally, in 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate, cementing his position as Rome's supreme leader.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to become Augustus?

questions.lessonTitle: The Pax Romana and Roman Peace
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period of approximately 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond with almost no warfare. This peace began with the reign of Augustus and lasted until the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE. More and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship during this time. The Pax Romana represented the height of Roman imperial power and stability, allowing for unprecedented economic growth, cultural exchange, and infrastructure development across the empire.
questions.question: How many years did the Pax Romana last?

questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After the death of Emperor Nero in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this chaotic period: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This period illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession in the Roman Empire, where the military often played the decisive role in selecting who would become emperor rather than following any clear hereditary or democratic process.
questions.question: The Year of the Four Emperors occurred during the reign of Nero.

questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine played a pivotal role in the history of Christianity through his Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the Roman Empire. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity before him. Constantine converted to Christianity on his deathbed, making him the first Roman emperor to embrace the faith. This relationship between Constantine and Christianity fundamentally changed the trajectory of the religion, leading to future Roman emperors also being Christians and eventually making Christianity the dominant religion of the empire.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Constantine's relationship with Christianity?
choices: He made Christianity the state religion immediately upon becoming emperor
He abolished Christianity and persecuted Christians throughout his reign
He issued the Edict of Milan legalizing Christianity and converted on his deathbed
He initially banned Christianity but later reversed his policy
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE established religious toleration, legalizing Christianity. Constantine converted to Christianity only on his deathbed, not making it the state religion immediately, nor persecuting Christians.

questions.lessonTitle: Transformation and Decline of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The transformation from a unified Roman Empire to the divided East/West structure began with Diocletian's administrative reforms. In 285 CE, Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) to strengthen governance. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople. Once Constantine established Constantinople as the new capital city, the east/west split deepened considerably. These three events represent the key steps in the transformation process that eventually led to the complete separation of the Western Roman Empire (which ended in 476 CE) and the Eastern Byzantine Empire (which lasted until 1453).
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative transformation of the Roman Empire?

questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marked the end of the ancient Roman state in the West. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The fall of the Western Roman Empire was preceded by centuries of economic troubles, military decline, political instability, and social changes that weakened the empire beyond recovery.
questions.question: In what year was the Western Roman Empire officially ended?

questions.lessonContent: Justinian was a powerful emperor of the Eastern (Byzantine) empire headquartered at Constantinople. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan. Justinian rewrote Roman law, creating the Corpus Juris Civilis, also known as the Justinian Code. This legal code still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today. The Justinian Code encapsulated more than 1,000 years of Roman legal development.
questions.question: The Corpus Juris Civilis, or Justinian Code, is still used as the basis for civil law in several countries today.

questions.lessonContent: Romance languages developed from Latin, which was the language of Rome. The main Romance languages include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. These languages evolved from Vulgar Latin, the everyday spoken Latin of ordinary Romans, rather than the classical Latin used in formal writing. The spread of these languages followed the expansion and eventual fragmentation of the Roman Empire across different regions of Europe.
questions.question: Which of the following is a Romance language that developed from Latin?
questions.explanation: Spanish is a Romance language (meaning 'Roman') that developed from Latin, along with French, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian. Old English and Anglo-Saxon were Germanic languages, not derived from Latin.

questions.lessonContent: Under Emperor Constantine, several pivotal steps transformed the Roman Empire's relationship with Christianity. First, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium. Second, he renamed the city Constantinople. Third, he issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration. Fourth, he converted to Christianity on his deathbed. These actions fundamentally changed Christianity's status from a persecuted faith to the dominant religion of the empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Constantine's transformation of the Roman Empire regarding Christianity?
choices: Convert to Christianity on his deathbed
Move capital from Rome to Byzantium
Issue the Edict of Milan (legalize Christianity)

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature uses an architecture where a lead agent plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different aspects of the question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. This parallel approach enables thorough, independent investigations while maintaining separation of concerns through distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories.
questions.question: According to the source content, what is a multi-agent system defined as?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations at Anthropic show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries involving multiple independent directions simultaneously. A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single-agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches. The performance gains come primarily from token usage, which alone explains 80% of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.
questions.question: The multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval.

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning a list of findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. In contrast to traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches that use static retrieval, this architecture uses multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers.
questions.question: What is the name of the architecture pattern used in Anthropic's Research system?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that the Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: One surprising finding was that Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers. When given a prompt and a failure mode, they can diagnose why the agent is failing and suggest improvements. Anthropic created a tool-testing agent that, when given a flawed MCP tool, attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures. This agent tests the tool dozens of times, finding key nuances and bugs in the process. The result was a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new description, because they were able to avoid most mistakes that the old description caused.
questions.question: What percentage decrease in task completion time did the tool-testing agent achieve for future agents using the improved description?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs provide a natural fit for grading these outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They experimented with multiple judges but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgments. This method was especially effective when eval test cases had clear answers.
questions.question: A single LLM call outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 with a pass-fail grade produces evaluations most aligned with human judgments.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: Agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. Using the right tool is often strictly necessary for success—for instance, an agent searching the web for context that only exists in Slack is doomed from the start. With MCP servers that give models access to external tools, agents encounter unseen tools with descriptions of wildly varying quality. Anthropic gave their agents explicit heuristics for tool selection: first, examine all available tools; second, match tool usage to user intent; third, search the web for broad external exploration; and fourth, prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a tool selection heuristic for agents?
choices: Search the web for broad external exploration
Match tool usage to user intent
Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for flexibility
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for flexibility' because the source explicitly states agents should 'prefer specialized tools over generic ones' as one of the four heuristics, making the opposite statement (preferring generic tools) the correct choice for what is NOT listed.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: When building reliable multi-agent systems, Anthropic follows a systematic evaluation approach. The process begins by starting evaluation immediately with small samples, as early agent development changes tend to have dramatic impacts and large effect sizes can be spotted with just a few test cases. Once initial testing is complete, the team uses LLM-as-judge for output evaluation to scalably evaluate hundreds of outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and citation accuracy. Finally, they apply human evaluation for edge cases, as people testing agents find issues that automated evals miss, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the agent evaluation workflow?
choices: Apply Human Evaluation for Edge Cases

questions.lessonTitle: Agent Error Recovery and State Management
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, errors compound because agents maintain state across many tool calls during long-running processes. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can become catastrophic for agents since restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. The solution involves building systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, rather than starting over from the beginning. Anthropic also uses the model’s intelligence to handle issues gracefully—for example, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and allowing it to adapt works surprisingly well. This combines the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: How does the system handle errors that occur during long-running agent processes?
questions.answer: The system resumes from where the agent was when the error occurred rather than restarting from the beginning, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and checkpoints

questions.lessonContent: Currently, Anthropic's lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents. With synchronous execution, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed, but would add challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents.
questions.question: The current lead agent implementation executes subagents synchronously.

questions.lessonTitle: Deployment Strategy for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This creates a deployment challenge because whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process. Deploying changes all at once would disrupt running agents and potentially lose their current state. To avoid this, engineers use a technique called rainbow deployments that gradually shifts traffic from old to new versions while keeping both versions running simultaneously. This ensures that agents in flight can complete their work without interruption while new agents spawn with the updated version.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent code changes from breaking existing agents mid-process?
choices: Blue-green deployments that switch all traffic at once
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions
Rolling deployments that update agents sequentially
Canary deployments that test on a small percentage of users
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, preventing disruptions to agents that are mid-process during deployment

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, and is available with 8 open source embeddings models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with options of 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers access to powerful embedding models at very competitive prices. According to the release announcement, these models can be accessed at prices that are up to 4x cheaper compared to other popular platforms.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers pricing that is up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes newly released M2-BERT retrieval models specifically designed for long context tasks. These models are available in three variants with different context lengths to handle various document sizes. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K variant has an embedding dimension of 768, which is used for data visualization tasks such as plotting sample data from RedPajama-v1 using tSNE transformation.
questions.question: Which of the following context length options are available for M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are explicitly stated to be available for long context with three options: 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example demonstrates how to work with Together Embeddings. First, you use the sample_and_extract_embeddings function to sample data examples from various data files. Then, you extract embeddings for each sampled example using the generate_embeddings function with the Together API. Finally, you transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors using tSNE to enable 2D visualization of the data.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings visualization workflow?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's service. To configure the connection, you need to specify the base URL as "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" when initializing the OpenAI client. This enables seamless migration of existing applications to the Together platform without major code restructuring. The client is initialized with your Together API key and the base URL pointing to Together's v1 embeddings endpoint.
questions.question: What is the base URL required to configure the OpenAI client for the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint has been designed with full OpenAI compatibility as a core feature. This means that developers can use the same OpenAI client library they are familiar with, simply by changing the base URL and API key. The compatibility extends to the entire API structure, including how embeddings are created and returned. This design choice significantly reduces the learning curve and migration effort for teams already using OpenAI's embedding services.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI compatibility, allowing applications built for OpenAI to easily switch to Together.

questions.lessonContent: Together AI provides integrations with popular frameworks and databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation systems. The supported integrations include MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex, which are three of the most widely used tools in the AI development community. These integrations allow developers to leverage Together's embedding models within their existing RAG pipelines. The documentation provides deep-dive tutorials for implementing RAG using each of these frameworks with Together's API.
questions.question: Which of the following frameworks are supported for building RAG applications with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that integrations are available with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG applications.

questions.lessonTitle: Configuring OpenAI-Compatible Client for Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: When setting up the OpenAI-compatible API for Together Embeddings, you first initialize the OpenAI client with your API key and configure the base_url endpoint to point to the Together API. After establishing this connection, you define a get_embedding function that handles text preprocessing and calls the embeddings.create API to generate embeddings. This setup enables seamless migration from OpenAI to Together's embedding services.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in configuring the OpenAI-compatible client for Together Embeddings?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, the embedding dimension is 768. This means each text embedded with this model produces a 768-dimensional vector. When visualizing such high-dimensional data, dimensionality reduction techniques like tSNE are needed to plot the data in 2D space.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors from embedding models is typically too large to easily visualize in their raw form. To plot each data example in 2D for visualization, we use tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the embedding vectors. The transform_tSNE function takes the embedding matrix and converts it to a lower-dimensional representation suitable for plotting with matplotlib.
questions.question: The tSNE dimensionality reduction technique is used to transform high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional representation for visualization.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These vector databases store the embeddings and enable semantic search capabilities for retrieval. The tutorial also covers building RAG using frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex.
questions.question: Which of the following vector databases are supported for building RAG applications with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that you can build RAG using Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example using Together Embeddings, the process involves three key sequential steps. First, the system reads data from a JSONL file and extracts text samples. Then, the Generate Embeddings API is used to convert the text into vector representations. Finally, the Transform tSNE step reduces the high-dimensional embedding vectors to 2D for visualization purposes.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data preprocessing pipeline for Together Embeddings visualization?

questions.lessonContent: Before training Composer 2, the Cursor research team evaluated several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2. They used three evaluations to select the base model: coding knowledge measured with FreshBench (a question-answer benchmark), state tracking measured with an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff, and codebase perplexity measured over their private monorepo. Based on these evaluations, they selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2, which is a 1.04T parameter model with 32B active parameters in a Mixture-of-Experts architecture.
questions.question: What base model was selected for Composer 2 continued pretraining?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends the Kimi K2.5 base model through a continued pretraining stage divided into three distinct phases. The first and most compute-intensive phase trains at 32k token sequence length. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that expands the context window to 256k tokens. Finally, a brief supervised fine-tuning phase focuses on targeted coding tasks. Training was performed using MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s GPUs with the AdamW optimizer.
questions.question: The three phases of Composer 2 continued pretraining are: (1) bulk compute at 32k token sequence length, (2) long-context extension to 256k sequence length, and (3) a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: When selecting a base model for continued pretraining, the Cursor team evaluated models using multiple internal benchmarks. FreshBench measures coding knowledge through question-answer pairs created from traces where Composer had to read library source code or perform web searches. State tracking benchmarks test the model's ability to understand past file edits, similar to the LoCoDiff benchmark. Codebase perplexity measures the model's coding intelligence by computing negative log-likelihood over their private monorepo using a rolling window. These internal evaluations, combined with inference performance considerations, guided the base model selection.
questions.question: Which of the following evaluation measures were used to select the base model for Composer 2?
choices: Only coding knowledge and codebase perplexity
Only coding knowledge and state tracking
Coding knowledge (FreshBench), state tracking, and codebase perplexity
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that three evaluations contributed to base model selection: coding knowledge measured with FreshBench, state tracking measured with an internal benchmark, and codebase perplexity measured over their private monorepo.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 involves extending the base model with a code-dominated data mix. This stage is divided into three distinct phases that must be completed in sequence. First, the bulk of compute is spent training at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. Second, a shorter long-context extension phase expands the model's context window to 256k sequence length. Finally, a brief supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase focuses on targeted coding tasks to prepare the model for downstream reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the continued pretraining stage of Composer 2?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons, the model uses the self-summarization technique introduced in Composer 1.5. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. At the same time, poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window.
questions.question: In the self-summarization technique used by Composer 2, how is the reward applied across chained generations?
questions.answer: The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. The system maintains stability by minimizing how off-policy the samples become. On the infrastructure side, this divergence is reduced via fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, similar to PipelineRL. Inference workers are capable of updating weights mid-rollout, which means later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy. To reduce further divergence between the sampling and training policy, the system replays MoE routing.
questions.question: True or False: Composer 2's RL training uses synchronous weight updates where weights are only synchronized after each training step completes.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. The problem distribution reflects the most common use cases. According to Figure 3, the RL training tasks are categorized into: Iterate On Feature, Debugging, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Devops, Migration, Deletion, and Other. Notably, this training distribution captures many aspects of software engineering that are absent from popular AI coding benchmarks.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a task category used in Composer 2's RL training distribution?
questions.explanation: Code Generation is not listed as one of the task categories in Figure 3. The actual categories include Debugging, Testing, Devops, and others like Iterate On Feature, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Code Review, Optimize, Migration, Deletion, and Other.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 reinforcement learning pipeline, the training loop follows a specific sequence. First, a problem is sampled from the training distribution. Then, multiple rollouts are simulated from the agent with different solutions. After that, rewards are computed based on the code's correctness, succinctness, and conformance to software engineering principles. Finally, advantages are calculated to determine how much better each rollout performed compared to the group average, and the model weights are updated accordingly.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training loop?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Unlike public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications. According to the technical report, CursorBench tasks have a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks?

questions.lessonContent: The application of coding agents has evolved rapidly, expanding from simple tightly-scoped edits to complex debugging and feature development. The technical report identifies four primary factors causing misalignment between public benchmark performance and real-world utility: Domain Mismatch, Prompt Over-specification, Data Contamination and Overfitting, and Narrow Evaluation Scope. Because public benchmarks are constructed from historical scrapes of open-source repositories, they are frequently leaked into model training mixtures, artificially inflating scores. This contamination issue affects the validity of public benchmark scores.
questions.question: True or False: Data contamination is identified as a factor causing misalignment between public benchmark performance and real-world utility.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Parallelism Configuration in RL Phase
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions. The report specifies different parallelism configurations for different training phases. For the continued pretraining phase, Composer 2 uses EP=8 and CP=2. For the RL phase, the configuration changes to support the different computational demands of reinforcement learning training.
questions.question: What is the Context Parallelism (CP) configuration used for the RL phase in Composer 2?
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that Composer 2 uses EP=8, CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase and EP=8, CP=8 for the RL phase. This configuration change reflects the different computational demands of RL training compared to continued pretraining.

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation process for CursorBench tasks follows a systematic workflow. First, for each task in CursorBench, we initialize the codebase environment and initial task prompt. Then, we run the Cursor agent exactly as it would execute in our production environment, which involves executing a rollout in the environment. Finally, we compute accuracy aggregated over all tasks across multiple passes of the evaluation set to reduce variance, and we also measure efficiency metrics like completion tokens, end-to-end latency, and inference cost.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation workflow?

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo or wherever you run claude from (the most common usage), where you can name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md in any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos, or in any child of the directory where you run claude, where Claude will pull it in on demand when you work with files in those child directories. Additionally, you can place CLAUDE.md in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to all your claude sessions.
questions.question: Where is the MOST COMMON location for placing a CLAUDE.md file?
questions.answer: the root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from)

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety, requesting permission for any action that might modify your system including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. There are four ways to manage the allowed tools list: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, or using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: You can manually edit your .claude/settings.json file to manage allowed tools, and this file can be checked into source control to share with your team.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md files are ideal for documenting various types of project-specific information that you want Claude to remember. The recommended content includes common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette such as branch naming and merge vs. rebase, developer environment setup details like which compilers work, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. There is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, but the recommendation is to keep them concise and human-readable.
