questions.question: In the asynchronous RL training for Composer 2, a prompt is never trained on more than once.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks that reflect the most common use cases in software engineering. The problem distribution captures many aspects of software engineering that are absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. According to Figure 3 in the report, the training distribution includes task categories such as iterate on feature, debugging, new feature, refactor, understanding codebase, documentation, testing, code review, optimize, devops, migration, deletion, and other categories. In later stages of training, simple heuristics such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: Which of the following is a task category included in the RL training distribution for Composer 2?
questions.explanation: According to Figure 3 in the content, the RL training tasks include 'Refactor' as one of the main categories. The other options (Competitive Programming, Algorithm Design, Data Structures) are not listed in the training distribution, which focuses on real-world software engineering tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three sequential phases to build a strong foundation for downstream RL training. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to establish base coding knowledge. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, which enables the model to handle longer codebases. Finally, a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks further specializes the model for real-world software engineering problems before proceeding to reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Composer 2's continued pretraining methodology?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Unlike public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7–10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are also more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185–3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks?

questions.lessonContent: The asynchronous RL training pipeline for Composer 2 operates in the single-epoch regime, which means the same prompt is never trained on twice. This design ensures each training sample is used only once during the entire reinforcement learning process, preventing overfitting to specific prompts and maintaining training diversity.
questions.question: In Composer 2's asynchronous RL training, a prompt is never trained on more than once.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench differs from public evaluation benchmarks like SWE-bench in several key ways. Public benchmarks are typically highly specified with narrow sets of correct solutions, while real developer requests are often under-specified and admit multiple valid approaches. Additionally, public benchmarks suffer from data contamination issues where training data leaks into test sets, and they focus predominantly on functional correctness rather than evaluating code quality, latency, and interactive agent behavior. CursorBench tasks have a median of 181 lines changed while SWE-bench has only 7–10 lines.
questions.question: Which of the following is a key difference between CursorBench and public benchmarks like SWE-bench?
choices: CursorBench tasks require substantially more code changes (median 181 vs 7-10 lines)
CursorBench tasks use highly specified prompts with narrow solution sets
CursorBench tasks primarily measure functional correctness only
CursorBench tasks are immune to data contamination issues
questions.explanation: CursorBench tasks require substantially more code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to only 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, reflecting greater real-world complexity.

questions.lessonContent: The online evaluation process for Composer 2 requires setting up dedicated infrastructure to ensure model behavior during evaluations exactly matches what end users experience. For each training step we want to evaluate, we first acquire a lease for an evaluation deployment, then automatically move GPUs to that deployment, and finally perform a cross-region weight sync of the evaluation checkpoint from the training cluster where it resides to the inference deployment. This ensures faithful evaluation of the model's performance.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the online evaluation deployment setup for Composer 2?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. There is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, but they should be kept concise and human-readable. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: What is the special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in multiple locations to apply to different scopes of your projects. You can place them in the root of your repo (the most common usage), in any parent directory of where you run claude (most useful for monorepos), in any child directory (which pulls files on demand when working with files in those child directories), and in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When placed in the home folder, it applies to all your Claude sessions. You can also name a file CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it if you want local-only settings that are not shared with your team.
questions.question: You can place CLAUDE.md files in your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) to apply them to all your Claude sessions.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system by default, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions. The content gives examples such as adding Edit to always allow file edits, Bash(git commit:*) to allow git commits, or mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate to allow navigating with the Puppeteer MCP server.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid method for managing allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code
Use the --tools CLI flag to enable tools
Use the /config command to modify settings
questions.explanation: The /permissions command is explicitly listed as one of the four ways to manage allowed tools in Claude Code, allowing you to add or remove tools from the allowlist during a session.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing Claude Code, you first need to create a CLAUDE.md file in your repository root or home folder. Once created, you add content to CLAUDE.md by manually writing information or using the # key to have Claude automatically incorporate instructions. After adding content, you should tune CLAUDE.md iteratively, experimenting with different instructions and refining them based on how well Claude follows them. This three-step process of creating, adding content, and tuning forms the foundation of customizing your Claude Code setup.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for setting up CLAUDE.md files in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports extended thinking mode through specific trigger phrases that allocate additional computation time. These phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system, progressing from 'think' to 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink'. Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use when evaluating alternatives more thoroughly. Using the word 'think' in your instructions triggers this extended thinking mode, giving Claude additional computation time to evaluate solutions more thoroughly before responding.
questions.question: What is the lowest-level keyword that triggers extended thinking mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Test-driven development (TDD) becomes particularly powerful with agentic coding tools like Claude Code. The workflow involves writing tests based on expected input/output pairs, then explicitly telling Claude not to write any implementation code at this stage. After confirming tests fail, you instruct Claude to write code that passes the tests without modifying the tests themselves. Claude will iterate through writing code, running tests, adjusting the code, and running tests again until all tests pass. This approach provides Claude with a clear target to iterate against, allowing it to make changes, evaluate results, and incrementally improve until success.
questions.question: When using the test-driven development workflow in Claude Code, you should explicitly tell Claude not to write implementation code until after the tests have been written and confirmed to fail.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code allocates different levels of thinking budget based on specific trigger phrases you use in your prompts. The system recognizes a hierarchy of phrases that correspond to increasing levels of computational resources allocated for problem-solving. When you need Claude to thoroughly evaluate alternatives before responding, you can use these trigger phrases to control how much additional thinking time it receives. The lowest level uses a simple keyword, while the highest level provides maximum computational budget for complex problem-solving.
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct hierarchy of thinking budget phrases in Claude Code, from lowest to highest?
choices: ultrathink < think harder < think hard < think
think < think hard < think harder < ultrathink
think hard < think < think harder < ultrathink
think < ultrathink < think hard < think harder
questions.explanation: The correct hierarchy from lowest to highest thinking budget is: 'think' < 'think hard' < 'think harder' < 'ultrathink'. Each progressive level allocates more thinking budget for Claude to use when evaluating alternatives.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for effectively using Claude Code. First, you should ask Claude to plan solution with think to trigger extended thinking mode, which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. Once you confirm the plan is reasonable, have Claude create plan document so that you can reset to this spot if the implementation doesn't go as expected. Finally, ask Claude to implement its solution in code, and explicitly verify the reasonableness of the solution as it implements pieces.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow when moving from planning to implementation?

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Lightweight Multi-Agent Parallelism
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees provide a lighter-weight alternative to multiple repository checkouts for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously. This approach allows you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, where each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For instance, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts. The basic workflow involves creating worktrees with git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a and then launching Claude in each worktree.
questions.question: In the git worktrees approach for multi-Claude workflows, what do multiple worktrees share that makes them lightweight compared to full repository checkouts?
questions.answer: They share the same Git history and reflog

questions.lessonContent: When using multiple Claude instances for code verification, it is important to have separate context for each instance to get better results than a single Claude handling everything. The recommended workflow involves having one Claude write code, then running /clear or starting a second Claude in another terminal to provide fresh context. The second Claude then reviews the first Claude's work without being influenced by the previous conversation. After receiving feedback, you start another Claude or /clear again to read both the code and review feedback, and have this third Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation of context often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything in one session.
questions.question: The /clear command should be run before starting a new Claude session to ensure independent verification.

questions.lessonTitle: Headless Mode Fanning Out Pattern for Large-Scale Tasks
questions.lessonContent: The headless mode fanning out pattern is designed for handling large migrations or analyses where many similar tasks need to be processed programmatically. The first step involves having Claude write a script to generate a task list, such as a list of 2,000 files that need to be migrated from framework A to framework B. The second step loops through each task, calling Claude programmatically for each one and giving it a specific task and a set of tools it can use. An example invocation would be: claude -p "migrate foo.py from React to Vue. When you are done, you MUST return the string OK if you succeeded, or FAIL if the task failed." --allowedTools Edit,Bash(git commit:*). The third step runs the script several times and refines the prompt to get the desired outcome. This approach scales Claude's capabilities across many independent operations.
questions.question: In the headless mode fanning out pattern, what format should Claude return to indicate task success or failure?
choices: OK if successful, or FAIL if failed
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: 'When you are done, you MUST return the string OK if you succeeded, or FAIL if the task failed.' This specific return format is required for the automation script to track results.

questions.lessonContent: The multi-Agent workflow for code review involves having separate Claude instances handle different tasks. First, you use Claude to write code. Then, you run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal to review the first Claude's work. Finally, you start another Claude to read both the code and review feedback, and have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Agent code review workflow?
choices: Have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback
Have the second Claude review the first Claude's work

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: An HD screenshot has 1920 × 1080 pixels, which equals 2,073,600 total pixels. Each pixel stores three numbers representing red, green, and blue color values, with each value ranging from 0 to 255. Since each color channel requires one byte of storage, each pixel needs 3 bytes. Multiplying the total pixels by 3 bytes gives 2,073,600 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes, which is approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single uncompressed image.
questions.question: What is the file size in bytes of an HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels, assuming 3 bytes per pixel?

questions.lessonContent: Images are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers that specify how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create the final color. These values range from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, meaning the maximum amount of that color. For example, the color rgb(255, 147, 41) represents an orange with full red, moderate green, and low blue. This RGB system is the foundation of how digital images represent color.
questions.question: In the RGB color model used for digital images, each color channel value ranges from 0 to 255.

questions.lessonTitle: The Two Approaches to Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to reducing image file sizes. The first approach is lossy compression, which throws away parts of the data that humans won't notice, trading some quality for smaller file sizes. The second approach is lossless compression, which preserves every single pixel perfectly while still achieving file size reduction through clever encoding. Lossy compression is used by formats like JPEG, while lossless compression is used by formats like PNG. These two ideas power not only image formats but also ZIP files, web traffic, and most of the internet's data transmission.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the two fundamental approaches to image compression?
choices: Lossy compression is used by PNG; lossless compression is used by JPEG
Lossy compression reduces color resolution; lossless compression increases file size
Lossy compression throws away data humans won't notice; lossless compression stores every pixel perfectly
Lossy compression preserves all details; lossless compression removes some data
questions.explanation: Lossy compression (like JPEG) deliberately removes data that humans are unlikely to perceive, while lossless compression (like PNG) keeps all original pixel data through clever encoding techniques.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG lossless compression pipeline uses three sequential techniques to shrink image files while preserving every pixel. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores only the differences, which are typically small numbers easier to compress. Second, LZ77 Pattern Search scans the filtered data for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references to earlier data. Third, Huffman Encoding assigns shorter binary codes to the most frequently occurring values, similar to how Morse code uses short signals for common letters. These three steps work together in sequence to achieve significant compression without any loss of image quality.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits fundamental characteristics of human vision to reduce file size without obvious quality loss. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but tend to blur color information together. You will notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It then reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice minor color shifts while preserving brightness details that you perceive more sharply.
questions.question: When JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, what does it exploit?
questions.answer: How human vision works (eyes resolve brightness in detail but blur color together)

questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Frequency Components and Block Processing
questions.lessonContent: After separating brightness from color, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG then throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact. This is why at high quality settings, you barely notice the difference between the original and compressed image.
questions.question: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details. True or false?

questions.lessonContent: With lossy compression like JPEG, you cannot get the original pixels back once the data is discarded. The tradeoff is often worth it because you can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference. However, when you crank up the compression level, you'll see blocking artifacts where fine details get lost. These artifacts appear as visible block boundaries in areas that should have smooth gradients. JPEG doesn't support alpha transparency, which is why PNG is preferred for graphics requiring transparency.
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of lossy compression like JPEG?
choices: The file size remains unchanged after compression
JPEG supports transparency through alpha channels
You cannot recover the original pixels after compression
Blocking artifacts only appear at low compression levels
questions.explanation: Lossy compression discards data that cannot be recovered, which is why you cannot get the original pixels back. This allows 10-20x file size reduction but creates blocking artifacts at high compression levels.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression uses several key steps to reduce file size while maintaining visual quality. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color. Then, it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components using DCT. Finally, it discards high-frequency details that human vision won't typically notice, keeping only the important low-frequency information.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG lossy compression?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering to predict each pixel based on its neighbors, storing differences instead of actual values. The prediction methods are: Sub (predict from the left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predict from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predict from the average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly pick between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and pick the one that compresses best. This approach works because adjacent pixels are usually similar, making the differences small numbers that are easier to compress.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method is best for horizontal gradients?

questions.lessonContent: After filtering, PNG uses the LZ77 algorithm to find repeated patterns in the data. LZ77 spots patterns like 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2... and replaces them with back-references that say "go back 5 values and copy 5." This reference is much smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this significantly reduces file size.
questions.question: The LZ77 algorithm in PNG maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data to reference repeated patterns.

questions.lessonContent: PNG files are organized into chunks, each with a specific purpose. The essential chunks include IHDR (image header with metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual compressed image data), and IEND (end marker). PNG also includes checksums to detect file corruption: each chunk has a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint of its data. When you open a PNG, the computer recalculates this fingerprint; if it doesn't match, the file is damaged. PNG also supports alpha transparency (RGBA uses 4 bytes per pixel), while JPEG does not.
questions.question: What is the purpose of CRC-32 checksums in PNG files?
choices: To compress the image data more efficiently
To determine which prediction method to use
To convert RGB values to alpha values
To detect if the file has been corrupted or damaged
questions.explanation: CRC-32 checksums provide a mathematical fingerprint for each chunk. When opening a PNG, the computer recalculates this fingerprint; if it doesn't match, the file is considered damaged or corrupted.

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression preserves every pixel while shrinking file size. The process uses three core techniques in sequence. First, filtering predicts each pixel based on its neighbors and stores only the differences. Then, LZ77 pattern finding detects repeated sequences in the data and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman encoding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the lossless compression core algorithm?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: From Republic to Empire - The Establishment and Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire lasted from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, but the term Roman Empire specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors. Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate then gave Octavian the name Augustus, meaning most high, and in 23 BCE made him consul for life.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: From Republic to Empire - The Establishment and Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Roman Senate. The Senate also granted him the title Princeps, meaning first citizen, which became the origin of the word prince. Additionally, he was given the title Imperator, meaning successful general, which is the origin of the word emperor. He also held the position of Pontifex Maximus, or chief religious leader, which is the origin of the word pontiff used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate in 23 BCE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: From Republic to Empire - The Establishment and Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: When Octavian became Augustus, he received multiple titles from the Senate that established his supreme authority. He was made Princeps, meaning first citizen, which is the origin of the word prince. He was also given the title Imperator, meaning successful general, which is the origin of the word emperor. Additionally, he held the position of Pontifex Maximus, meaning chief religious leader, which is the origin of the word pontiff. He also held the power to call the Senate, veto the Senate's laws, and make laws himself.
questions.question: Which of the following titles granted to Augustus means first citizen?
questions.explanation: Princeps means first citizen and was the title Augustus used to maintain the illusion that he was an equal among senators rather than a dictator.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: From Republic to Empire - The Establishment and Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the undisputed ruler of Rome. The Senate then honored him by granting him the name Augustus, meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, the Senate made him consul for life, cementing his authority. These three events marked the transition from the Roman Republic to the Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Empire at Its Height - Emperors and Expansion
questions.lessonTitle: The Pax Romana: Duration and Extent
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, describes a period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, achieving complete control that resulted in almost no warfare. This remarkable peace lasted nearly 200 years, from 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship, extending the benefits of Roman governance to diverse populations across the empire. The Pax Romana is considered one of the longest periods of peace in recorded history.
questions.question: How long did the Pax Romana last?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Empire at Its Height - Emperors and Expansion
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After the death of Emperor Nero in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this chaotic year: Galba first, then Otho, followed by Vitellius, and finally Vespasian who emerged victorious. This rapid succession of rulers illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession that plagued the Roman Empire. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, rather than following any clear hereditary or legal process.
questions.question: The Year of the Four Emperors occurred in 69 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Empire at Its Height - Emperors and Expansion
questions.lessonTitle: Emperor Trajan's Expansion of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Trajan was born into a non-patrician family in what is now Spain, making him one of the first emperors from the provinces. He oversaw a massive public works program in Rome that included Trajan's Column, Trajan's Forum, and Trajan's Market. Under Trajan's leadership, the Roman Empire expanded to its greatest territorial extent, achieving the maximum expansion in the empire's history. Trajan is widely considered to have been one of the great emperors of Rome, balancing military conquest with public works and administration.
questions.question: Which Roman emperor expanded the empire to its greatest extent?
questions.explanation: Trajan (98-117 CE) oversaw the expansion of the Roman Empire to its greatest extent, which is why he is considered one of the great emperors.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Empire at Its Height - Emperors and Expansion
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. First, Galba became emperor after being declared as such by the Senate. However, Otho overthrows Galba shortly after, becoming the new emperor. Vitellius then defeats Otho in battle, taking control of Rome. Finally, Vespasian defeats Vitellius and establishes a new dynasty.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marked the final collapse of Roman political power in the west. The Eastern Roman Empire, also known as the Byzantine Empire, continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The division between east and west had begun when Emperor Diocletian split the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE to strengthen administration, and this split deepened after Constantine established Constantinople as the eastern capital.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Roman economy faced several critical problems that contributed to the empire's decline. There was a significant gap between the rich and the poor, with impoverished workers becoming tied to the land as coloni who were sold along with the land they worked. As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to buy goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined significantly. Additionally, large estates became self-sufficient, which further hurt manufacturing and trade by reducing the need for goods from outside sources.
questions.question: The Roman Empire experienced economic decline due to four main factors: (1) a gap between rich and poor, (2) the coloni system, (3) lack of purchasing power among the lower classes, and (4) self-sufficient estates. True or False?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian, who ruled the Byzantine Empire from 527 to 565 CE, made significant contributions to Roman legal history. Herewrite Roman law in what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This compilation encapsulated over a thousand years of Roman legal developments, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. The Justinian Code still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today, particularly in Europe.
questions.question: What major contribution did Emperor Justinian make to Roman law?
choices: He abolished all existing Roman legal traditions
He rewrote Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code)
He created the first Roman law during the Republic
questions.explanation: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law and remains the basis for civil law in several European countries today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire went through a gradual process of decline. Emperor Diocletian first divided the empire into administrative halves in 285 CE to make governance easier. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium (renamed Constantinople), further shifting power eastward. These administrative changes ultimately led to the permanent division of the empire and its eventual collapse in the West.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative division and fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: Diocletian divides the empire into east and west
Constantine moves the capital to Constantinople
The Western Roman Empire ends in 476 CE

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: What is a Multi-Agent Research System
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs that autonomously use tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature built by Anthropic uses an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Systems with multiple agents introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation, and reliability that differ from single-agent systems. The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously.
questions.question: What is the definition of a multi-agent system according to this content?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Agent Systems Outperform Single Agents Significantly
questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations conducted by Anthropic show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. Their multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches. Token usage itself explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other explanatory factors.
questions.question: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research evaluation.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Comparison in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In the Anthropic multi-agent research system, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than standard chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token consumption is a known downside that requires tasks with sufficient value to justify the increased performance costs. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance. Some domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.
questions.question: How many times more tokens do multi-agent systems use compared to standard chat interactions?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, while agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent research system workflow, the LeadResearcher first creates specialized Subagents with specific research tasks. These Subagents then independently perform web searches in parallel, exploring different aspects of the question simultaneously. Finally, the LeadResearcher synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed before proceeding to citation generation.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research workflow involving subagent creation, parallel search, and synthesis?

questions.lessonTitle: The Orchestrator-Worker Pattern in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The lead agent acts as an orchestrator that decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different aspects of the question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. This architecture enables parallel reasoning and information gathering across multiple specialized agents.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does the Anthropic Research system use?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than standard chat interactions due to their parallel processing and extended research capabilities. In their data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token usage is a fundamental characteristic of multi-agent architectures because they distribute work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic discovered that the Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers when given appropriate guidance. When presented with a prompt and a failure mode, they can diagnose why the agent is failing and suggest improvements to the prompt. They even created a tool-testing agent that, when given a flawed MCP tool, attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures. By testing the tool dozens of times, this agent found key nuances and bugs that would have otherwise gone unnoticed. This self-improvement process for improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new description, because they were able to avoid most mistakes.
questions.question: Which prompt engineering principle involves allowing Claude 4 models to improve prompts and tool descriptions when given a failure mode?
choices: Teach the orchestrator how to delegate
questions.explanation: The principle 'Let agents improve themselves' describes how Claude 4 models can diagnose failure modes and suggest improvements to prompts and tool descriptions. The tool-testing agent they created found key nuances and bugs, resulting in a 40% decrease in task completion time.

questions.lessonContent: When building effective multi-agent systems, agents need explicit heuristics for tool selection. The first step is to examine all available tools in the system. Then, agents must match tool usage to user intent, ensuring they select the most appropriate tools for the specific task. Finally, each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description to prevent agents from going down wrong paths.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the tool selection and design workflow?

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times). They found that a single LLM call with a prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: What are the five criteria used in the LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric for research outputs?
questions.answer: factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency

questions.lessonContent: Traditional evaluations often assume that the AI follows the same steps each time: given input X, the system should follow path Y to produce output Z. However, multi-agent systems don't work this way because even with identical starting points, agents might take completely different valid paths to reach their goal. One agent might search three sources while another searches ten, or they might use different tools to find the same answer. Since we don't always know what the right steps are, we usually can't just check if agents followed the prescribed steps in advance. Instead, flexible evaluation methods are needed that judge whether agents achieved the right outcomes while also following a reasonable process.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems can be evaluated the same way as traditional AI systems by checking if agents followed the exact steps prescribed in advance.

questions.lessonContent: In traditional software, a bug might break a feature, degrade performance, or cause outages. In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means we need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents because when errors occur, we cannot simply restart from the beginning as restarts are expensive and frustrating for users.
questions.question: Which of the following is identified as a key production reliability challenge for multi-agent systems?
choices: The compound nature of errors where minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes
The inability to use parallel tool calling for performance optimization
The lack of need for context management in long-running conversations
The simplicity of debugging non-deterministic agent behavior
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'The compound nature of errors in agentic systems means that minor issues for traditional software can derail agents entirely.' This is the key production reliability challenge mentioned for multi-agent systems.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024. This announcement marked the introduction of 8 open-source embedding models to the Together AI platform. The release included top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models. These models were positioned as achieving state-of-the-art performance with comparable or better accuracy than closed models. The pricing was advertised as very competitive, up to 4 times cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: On what date was the Together Embeddings endpoint released?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI compatibility to facilitate easy migration for developers. This compatibility means that developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API can easily switch to the Together endpoint by changing the base URL. The base URL for the Together API is "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". This OpenAI compatibility is a specific feature highlighted in the announcement to make migrating existing applications straightforward.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully compatible with the OpenAI API, allowing easy migration for existing applications.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Length Options for M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers M2-BERT retrieval models with varying context lengths to handle different retrieval tasks. These long context models are designed to significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. The available context length options for M2-BERT retrieval models are 2k, 8k, and 32k. This means users can generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: What are the available context length options for M2-BERT retrieval models on the Together platform?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are explicitly available with context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k as stated in the source content.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: The Purpose of Retrieval Augmented Generation
questions.lessonContent: There has been an increasing interest in retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models. Specifically, RAG addresses the problem of a lack of knowledge from unseen data by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base. This is accomplished through embeddings, which measure the similarity or relatedness of text queries. The retrieved relevant information is then provided to a generative model to produce more accurate and contextually aware responses.
questions.question: What limitation of generative AI models does RAG aim to overcome?
questions.answer: a lack of knowledge from unseen data

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: Frameworks for Building RAG with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Beyond vector databases, RAG applications can also be built by leveraging frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. These frameworks provide abstraction layers that simplify the process of connecting embedding generation, vector storage, and retrieval. They also offer integrations with the Together API, making it straightforward to swap in Together's embedding models. Developers can follow tutorials specifically dedicated to building RAG using Together with LangChain or using Together with LlamaIndex.
questions.question: True or False: LangChain and LlamaIndex are mentioned as frameworks that can be used to build RAG applications with Together Embeddings.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: Vector Databases Compatible with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embedding models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These vector databases store the embeddings and enable efficient similarity search over large document collections. When a query comes in, the system generates an embedding for that query and retrieves the most similar documents from the vector database.
questions.question: Which of the following vector databases can be used with Together Embeddings to build RAG applications?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that you can build RAG using Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma.

questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model is specifically designed for long context retrieval tasks and produces embedding vectors with a dimension of 768. This dimensionality is too large to easily visualize in its raw form, which is why dimensionality reduction techniques like tSNE are necessary to plot the data in two-dimensional space. The code uses the API string "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval" to generate these embeddings from sample text data.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.lessonContent: The visualization code uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional space suitable for plotting. The transform_tSNE function takes parameters including n_components (set to 2 for 2D visualization) and perplexity (set to 15 in the example). This allows data points from different sources to be plotted on a scatter plot while preserving their relative relationships from the original high-dimensional space.
questions.question: True or False: The code uses tSNE to transform embedding vectors for 2D visualization.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example uses sample data from the RedPajama-v1 dataset across five different domains. The code processes five JSONL files: arxiv_sample.jsonl (academic papers), book_sample.jsonl (book texts), c4_sample.jsonl (web corpus), github_sample.jsonl (code repositories), and stackexchange_sample.jsonl (Q&A forum posts). The visualization displays these as different colored clusters, with the results showing that texts from each source are somewhat closely located, revealing similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4.
questions.question: Which of the following file lists matches the five data sources used in the visualization example?
questions.explanation: The example explicitly uses arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl as the five data source filenames.

questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example from the Together Embeddings endpoint documentation, the process involves several key steps. First, the code reads data from JSONL files using the sample_and_extract_embeddings function. Then, it generates embeddings for each text example by calling the generate_embeddings function with the Together API. Finally, to make the high-dimensional embeddings (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) visualizable in 2D, the code applies tSNE transformation using the transform_tSNE function.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data visualization pipeline using Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonContent: The base model selected for Composer 2 was Kimi K2.5, which is a Mixture-of-Experts model with specific parameter configurations. According to the technical report, Kimi K2.5 has 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters. This model was chosen after evaluating several potential open-source base models including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2, using internal evaluations measuring coding knowledge, state tracking, and codebase perplexity.
questions.question: What is the total parameter count of the Kimi K2.5 base model used for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's continued pretraining is divided into three distinct phases with different sequence lengths. The bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that increases the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, there is a short supervised fine-tuning phase focused on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to progressively handle longer contexts while maintaining coding capabilities.
questions.question: The long-context extension phase uses a 256k token sequence length.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer team evaluated three base models for continued pretraining: Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, and GLM-5. They used three internal benchmarks for evaluation. FreshBench measures factual coding knowledge through question-answer pairs created from traces where Composer had to read library source code or perform web searches. State tracking measures the model's ability to recreate file states after many diffs, using an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff. Codebase perplexity measures the model's coding intelligence by computing negative log-likelihoods over the private monorepo. Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, a state tracking score of 86, and a negative log-likelihood of 13.81M.
questions.question: Which base model achieved the highest FreshBench score among the three models evaluated?
questions.explanation: Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, which was the highest score among the three evaluated open-source base models (DeepSeek V3.2 at 68.9% and GLM-5 at 79.2%). GPT-5.4 achieved 92.5% but was not among the base models considered for training.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 involves multiple phases to progressively improve the model's coding capabilities. First, the model spends the bulk of compute at a 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that expands the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks is applied to specialize the model for specific coding challenges. This staged approach ensures the model develops both broad knowledge and specialized skills.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three main phases in the Composer 2 continued pretraining process?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. The problem distribution reflects the most common use cases in software engineering. According to Figure 3, the training distribution includes task categories such as Iterate On Feature, Debugging, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Devops, Migration, Deletion, and Other. Notably, this training distribution captures many aspects of software engineering that are absent from popular AI coding benchmarks.
questions.question: Which task category represents the largest portion of RL training tasks in Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: A growing body of recent literature has argued that RL on LLMs often improves average performance primarily by concentrating probability mass on already-known successful trajectories, sometimes at the cost of policy entropy and output diversity. Under this view, improvements at best-of-K may be limited because the model becomes better at selecting one high-confidence solution rather than expanding the set of reachable correct solutions. However, against this backdrop, Composer 2's results are notable: rather than observing a trade-off in which average reward rises while best-of-K remains flat, the training improves both statistics as shown in Figure 5. This suggests that, in this setting, RL is not merely reweighting a fixed pool of reasoning paths, but is also improving the model's effective coverage of correct solutions under repeated sampling.
questions.question: According to the technical report, RL training for Composer 2 improved both average reward and best-of-K performance simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: While the primary goal of RL training is to improve model intelligence, the training process also aims to produce a model that provides a good developer experience. This is affected by the communication style of the model as well as the time and resources it takes to answer a question. To shape behavior and communication, an array of auxiliary rewards are applied to ensure the model provides a good experience. These include rewards for coding style, communication, and product-specific penalties for poor tool calls, such as creating to-do list items and then leaving them unfinished. During RL training, the model is monitored for emergent behaviors and occasionally additional behavior rewards are introduced as needed.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of applying auxiliary rewards in Composer 2's reinforcement learning training?
choices: To reduce the cost of serving the model at inference time
To improve the model's performance on public coding benchmarks
To ensure the model provides a good developer experience through communication style and response efficiency
To increase the model's parameter count for better intelligence
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that auxiliary rewards are applied to ensure the model provides a good developer experience, which is affected by communication style and the time and resources needed to answer a question.

questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training, the process begins by sampling a problem from our distribution. The model then generates rollouts by executing actions in the environment. After rollouts are collected, we compute rewards based on code correctness, succinctness, and conformance to software engineering principles. Finally, we calculate advantages using these rewards to update the policy.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the reinforcement learning rollout and advantage computation process?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is evaluated on CursorBench, an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. According to the technical report, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench. This represents a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 which scored 44.2%, and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 which scored 38.0%. The CursorBench evaluation uses the same Cursor harness that is used by the deployed model, with equivalent tools and structure, providing high confidence that model behavior during evaluations is an exact replication of what end users see.
questions.question: What is the accuracy score achieved by Composer 2 on CursorBench?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. According to Figure 7 in the technical report, CursorBench tasks have a median of 181 lines changed in reference diffs. In contrast, SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual require only 7-10 lines changed. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering, where developers must frequently synthesize context from production logs, sparse user bug reports, and large existing codebases to derive a solution.
questions.question: CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications than public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis instead of Tensor Parallelism (TP) which was used in previous Composer training stacks. CP requires less communication than TP and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections. The technical report states that Composer 2 uses CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase and CP=8 for the RL phase. Additionally, the context parallelism dimension is folded into the FSDP dimension, allowing CP ranks to reduce per-GPU parameter and state memory usage.
questions.question: Which parallelism method does Composer 2 use as the primary long-context scaling axis?
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that "Composer 2 instead uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis" because "CP requires less communication than TP and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections."

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 introduced significant changes to the parallelism architecture compared to previous Composer training stacks. The original design combined Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP), Expert Parallelism (EP), and Tensor Parallelism (TP) where EP reused the same rank group as TP, making EP not an independent scaling axis. Composer 2 then introduced Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis which requires less communication than TP and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions. Finally, Composer 2 implemented a more flexible expert-parallel design by decoupling EP from TP, which requires using different meshes for sharding dense layers and expert weights.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the evolution of parallelism architecture in Composer 2 training infrastructure?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This file can be placed in multiple locations to customize your setup: the root of your repository (the most common usage), any parent directory of where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child directory (where Claude will pull it in on demand when working with files in those directories), or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. The file can be named CLAUDE.md and checked into git for team sharing, or named CLAUDE.local.md and added to .gitignore for personal use. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md file for you.
questions.question: In which location can CLAUDE.md files be stored? (Choose all that apply)
questions.answer: root of your repo, any parent directory, any child directory, your home folder (~/.claude/)

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach, requesting permission for any action that might modify your system including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. There are four ways to manage the allowed tools list: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command to add or remove tools after starting Claude Code, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (with the former recommended for team sharing), or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions. When using the /permissions command, you can add tools such as Edit to always allow file edits, Bash(git commit:*) to allow git commits, or mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate to allow navigating with the Puppeteer MCP server.
questions.question: Claude Code's /permissions command explicitly mentions adding Edit to always allow file edits as a possible tool management action.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Claude Code for Your Workflow
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, connecting to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that specific directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file that makes the tools available to anyone working in your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box. When working with MCP, using the --mcp-debug flag can help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: When configuring MCP servers in Claude Code, what are the three ways to make them available?
choices: In the CLAUDE.md file, in global config, and in environment variables
In the root directory, in parent directories, and in child directories
In project config, in global config, and in a checked-in .mcp.json file
In the .claude/settings.json file, in the ~/.claude.json file, and in a .mcp.json file
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file (available to anyone working in your codebase).

questions.lessonTitle: Triggering Extended Thinking in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, using specific trigger words activates extended thinking mode, giving Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. The system recognizes four distinct phrases mapped to progressively increasing thinking budgets: the word "think" provides a baseline level, "think hard" increases it further, "think harder" provides even more computational resources, and "ultrathink" allocates the maximum thinking budget available. The more complex or important the problem, the more benefit comes from using a higher-level trigger word. This feature is particularly valuable during the planning phase of any workflow before diving into implementation.
questions.question: What word should you use to trigger extended thinking mode when asking Claude to make a plan?

questions.lessonContent: The test-driven development workflow for Claude Code involves five distinct steps that must be completed in sequence. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input and output pairs while explicitly stating you're doing TDD. Second, you instruct Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly telling it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Third, you have Claude commit the tests when satisfied. Fourth, Claude writes code to pass the tests without modifying them, iterating until all tests pass. Fifth, you ask Claude to commit the code once satisfied with the changes. This workflow leverages Claude's ability to iterate toward a clear target.
questions.question: In the test-driven development workflow, Claude should be explicitly told not to write any implementation code until after the tests have been written and confirmed to fail.

questions.lessonContent: Advanced workflows with multiple Claude instances can be implemented through several approaches. The simplest method involves one Claude writing code while another reviews or tests it in a separate terminal, using /clear or starting fresh to maintain separate context. A heavier-weight but more efficient approach uses git worktrees, which allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories while sharing Git history. Git worktrees enable running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on independent tasks without merge conflicts. Another approach creates multiple git checkouts in separate folders, opening each in different terminal tabs with different tasks.
questions.question: Which of the following is mentioned as a lighter-weight alternative to multiple repository checkouts when running multiple Claude sessions?
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog, making them lighter-weight than maintaining separate full repository checkouts.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for solving many problems with Claude Code. First, you should ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs to understand the problem space. Next, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem, preferably using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode. After the plan is confirmed, ask Claude to implement the solution in code. Finally, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request, updating any relevant documentation.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow?

questions.lessonContent: One effective pattern involves having one Claude instance write code while another reviews or tests it. This approach works because separate Claude sessions maintain independent contexts, similar to how multiple engineers might collaborate. The workflow proceeds as follows: first, use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work, start another Claude to read both the code and review feedback, and finally have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything. Some engineers even use this pattern with tests, where one Claude writes tests and another writes code to make the tests pass.
questions.question: In the multiClaude verification pattern, what command should you run before starting a second Claude to review the first Claude's work?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode specifically designed for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and other automation tasks. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag combined with a prompt. For streaming JSON output, you can use the --output-format stream-json flag. It's important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each session rather than having it carry over. This mode is particularly useful for powering automations triggered by GitHub events, such as inspecting new issues as they come in and assigning appropriate labels.
questions.question: True or false: Claude Code's headless mode persists between sessions automatically once enabled.

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees provide a lighter-weight alternative to multiple repository checkouts for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. To use this approach, you first create worktrees using the command 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', then launch Claude in each worktree by running 'cd ../project-feature-a && claude'. You can create additional worktrees as needed by repeating these steps in new terminal tabs. Some best practices include using consistent naming conventions, maintaining one terminal tab per worktree, setting up notifications for when Claude needs attention, using separate IDE windows for different worktrees, and cleaning up when finished using 'git worktree remove ../project-feature-a'.
questions.question: What is the correct command to create a git worktree for a feature branch?
questions.explanation: The correct command is 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', which creates a new worktree directory at the specified path and checks out the given branch into it.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-Claude verification workflow, the process begins with the first Claude using its agentic capabilities to write code. Once the initial code is complete, you run /clear or start a second Claude instance to review the work independently. The second Claude then reviews the first Claude's code. Finally, you start another Claude to read both the code and the review feedback, enabling this Claude to edit the code based on the feedback provided. This sequential process ensures thorough verification through isolated review cycles.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude verification workflow?
choices: Have this Claude edit code based on feedback

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three color values representing red, green, and blue, with each value ranging from 0 (no color) to 255 (maximum intensity). For an HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, the total number of pixels is 2,073,600. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes (one byte each for R, G, and B), the raw file size calculates to 6,220,800 bytes, which equals approximately 6.2 megabytes.
questions.question: What is the approximate file size in megabytes of an uncompressed HD screenshot (1920 × 1080 pixels) with 3 bytes per pixel?

questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to image compression. Lossy compression works by throwing away parts of the image that humans won't notice, trading some quality for significantly smaller file sizes. Lossless compression takes a different approach by being clever about how every pixel is stored, preserving every exact pixel while still achieving some size reduction. These two ideas power common formats like JPEG, PNG, and ZIP files, as well as web traffic and most of the internet's data transfer.
questions.question: Lossy compression preserves every single pixel of the original image while reducing file size.

questions.lessonTitle: Pixel Color Representation in Digital Images
questions.lessonContent: Digital images are constructed from tiny colored squares known as pixels. Each pixel in a standard RGB image contains three numerical values that determine its color: the amount of red, the amount of green, and the amount of blue. These color values range from 0, representing the absence of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. By mixing these three color channels at different intensities, pixels can produce the full spectrum of colors seen in digital images.
questions.question: What three color values does each pixel in a standard RGB image store?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that each pixel is three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with values ranging from 0 to 255.

questions.lessonContent: In PNG lossless compression, the data goes through three main compression stages in sequence. First, filtering or prediction stores the differences between pixels rather than their absolute values, making the data more uniform. Second, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences in the sliding window and replaces them with back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values. These three steps must be applied in this exact order to achieve optimal compression.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three core compression stages in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Transformation in Lossy Compression
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in photographs, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs contain mostly smooth gradients, most information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG then throws away the high-frequency details that human vision won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact. This block-based transformation is what gives compressed images their characteristic artifacts when compression is too high.
questions.question: Into how many pixel blocks does JPEG divide the image for transformation?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression (used by JPEG) exploits how human vision works by throwing away data that humans won't notice. The human eye resolves brightness in fine detail but blurs color together. JPEG takes advantage of this by separating brightness from color and reducing color resolution. With lossy compression, you can't get the original pixels back once the data is thrown away. The tradeoff is often worth it: 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference.
questions.question: Lossy compression can restore the original pixel values after compression.

questions.lessonTitle: The Color and Brightness Separation in JPEG
questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses a clever approach to compression by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color.
