results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Research work involves open-ended problems where it is very difficult to predict the required steps in advance, making AI agents particularly well-suited for these tasks due to the flexibility required to pivot or explore tangential connections as investigations unfold. The model must operate autonomously for many turns, making decisions about which directions to pursue based on intermediate findings. This unpredictability means a linear, one-shot pipeline cannot handle these complex research tasks.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A system consisting of multiple LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop that work together to accomplish tasks

questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations by Anthropic show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries involving pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. A specific evaluation tested a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents against a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system. The multi-agent system outperformed the single-agent system by 90.2% on the internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found correct answers by decomposing the task into subtasks for subagents operating in parallel, while the single-agent system failed with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research evaluation.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, revealed that three factors explained 95% of the performance variance. Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice being the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates the multi-agent architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. In practice, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than standard chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chats. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 provides a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
questions.question: What percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation was explained by token usage alone?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the other two factors that together explain the remaining 15%.

questions.lessonTitle: Lead Agent Responsibilities in the Research Architecture
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The LeadResearcher enters an iterative research process, beginning by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context. Each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the lead agent for synthesis.
questions.question: What is the primary role of the lead agent in the Research system architecture?
questions.answer: To coordinate the research process by analyzing queries, developing strategies, and spawning specialized subagents to explore different aspects of a query in parallel

questions.lessonContent: In the Research system architecture, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents in real-time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. While this synchronous approach simplifies error handling and result coordination, it limits the system's ability to dynamically adapt during the research process.
questions.question: The Research system uses synchronous execution, meaning the lead agent waits for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding to the next step.

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Variance Factors in BrowseComp Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: In analyzing what makes browsing agents effective, Anthropic found that three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation. This evaluation tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information across the web. Their analysis revealed that token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance, making it the dominant factor. The two additional explanatory factors were the number of tool calls made by the agent and the model choice, which refers to which Claude model was used. This finding validated their architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning.
questions.question: Which three factors together explain 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation?
choices: Token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice
Number of subagents, query complexity, and response length
Token usage, search depth, and source quality
Model choice, tool selection, and context window size
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation... token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors.'

questions.lessonTitle: Agent State Management and Error Recovery
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. This means engineers need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents, because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combining the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What approach did Anthropic build to handle errors in their multi-agent system without requiring expensive restarts?
questions.answer: Systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, combined with retry logic and checkpoints

questions.lessonTitle: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Execution in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Currently, Research lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: In the current Research system architecture, lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete before proceeding. This design creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic used multiple evaluation approaches for their research agents. For LLM-as-judge evaluation, they used a single LLM call with a prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade, evaluating outputs against criteria including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They also started with small samples of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns, which allowed them to spot dramatic impacts from changes in early development. Human evaluation was essential for catching edge cases like hallucinated answers on unusual queries and source selection biases where agents chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative sources.
questions.question: Which evaluation method did Anthropic use that involved a single LLM call outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade to evaluate outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and source quality?
questions.explanation: Anthropic used an LLM-as-judge evaluation where a single LLM call with a single prompt output scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade, evaluating outputs against criteria including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Model Selection
questions.lessonTitle: Purpose and Applications of Text Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. They are used for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification. Additionally, embeddings are fundamental to retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data. RAG finds relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and provides this information to a generative model. The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 leading embedding models that achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB benchmarks.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide a measure of?
questions.answer: similarity or relatedness of given text queries

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Model Selection
questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Capabilities of M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context capabilities, available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. These M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. This means users can generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. The M2-Retrieval models represent state-of-the-art long context options within the Together platform.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models are available in context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Model Selection
questions.lessonTitle: Selecting Embedding Models from the Together Platform
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 open source embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. Some of these models outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks. When selecting an embedding model, users should consider their specific use case and whether they need long context capabilities (M2-BERT models) or standard context support.

questions.explanation: UAE-Large-v1 is explicitly listed as one of the top models from the MTEB leaderboard available in the Together Embeddings endpoint. The other options are not embedding models offered by Together AI.

Then, we transform the embedding vectors using tSNE to reduce the high-dimensional embeddings to 2D for visualization. To configure the client, users need to set the base_url to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" along with their Together API key. This integration approach simplifies migration from other platforms while maintaining similar code structure.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings supports integrations with popular frameworks and databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation systems. Specifically, the platform offers integration capabilities with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG implementations. These integrations enable developers to connect embeddings with vector databases and leverage established frameworks for building AI applications.

Each variant has a specific API string used to identify the model when making requests. The 8k context model specifically uses the API string "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval" as demonstrated in the data visualization code example provided in the documentation.

questions.lessonTitle: API Integration and Code Implementation - Embedding Generation Process
questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint to generate embeddings, the process involves several key sequential steps. First, you need to Initialize the API Client to establish the connection to the Together API. Then, you must Set the Model API String to specify which embedding model to use (such as togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval). Finally, you Call the Embeddings Create API to send the input text and receive the embedding response. These three steps form the core of the embedding generation workflow using the Together API.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. RAG aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model. You can build RAG using Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma or by leveraging frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. This approach allows generative models to access up-to-date or specialized information that was not part of their original training data.
questions.question: What does Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) aim to overcome in generative AI models?
questions.answer: a lack of knowledge from unseen data

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768. To plot each data example in 2D, we will use tSNE to transform the embedding vectors. The tSNE function takes an embedding matrix with n samples by m dimensions and transforms it to n by n_components, allowing high-dimensional embeddings to be displayed in a two-dimensional space. This dimensionality reduction technique preserves the relative relationships between data points when projecting them into visual space.

The visualization used sample data from RedPajama-v1, including arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, and github_sample.jsonl. When visualized using t-SNE, texts from each data source are somewhat closely located, showing that embeddings capture domain-specific patterns. The visualization also revealed similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are shown to be less related. This demonstrates how embedding visualization can help identify clustering and semantic relationships in datasets.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Kimi K2.5 as its base model, which is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. The model has 1.04 trillion total parameters with 32 billion active parameters. This base model was selected after evaluating several open-source models including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2, using internal evaluations measuring coding knowledge (FreshBench), state tracking capabilities, and codebase perplexity on the private monorepo.
questions.question: What is the name and parameter configuration of the base model used for Composer 2?
questions.answer: Kimi K2.5 with 1.04T parameters and 32B active parameters

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, specifically the Kimi K2.5 model. MoE models use a routing mechanism where different tokens are processed by different 'expert' networks, allowing the model to efficiently scale its total parameter count while only activating a subset of parameters for each inference. The Kimi K2.5 base model combines 1.04 trillion total parameters with 32 billion active parameters per token.
questions.question: Composer 2 is built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that enable it to perform software engineering tasks. These tools allow the model to read and edit files directly in the codebase, run shell commands for executing code and scripts, search the codebase using both grep pattern matching and semantic search capabilities, and search the web for external information. The model's prompt includes a system message, tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task prompt.
questions.question: Which of the following tools is Composer 2 NOT described as having access to?
choices: Compile and execute code in isolated sandbox environments
Search the codebase using grep or semantic search
questions.explanation: While Composer 2 can run shell commands, it does not specifically have a tool described as 'compile and execute code in isolated sandbox environments.' The tools explicitly mentioned are reading/editing files, running shell commands, grep/semantic search, and web search. The 'compile and execute' capability is not listed as a distinct tool in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. We divide this stage into three phases. We spend the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the Composer 2 continued pretraining pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. The bulk of computational resources are allocated to the first phase, which trains at a 32k token sequence length. This is followed by a significantly shorter second phase that extends the context length to 256k tokens. The final phase consists of a brief supervised fine-tuning stage focused on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to first build foundational coding knowledge before gradually expanding its long-context capabilities.
questions.question: What is the sequence length used in the bulk of Composer 2's continued pretraining compute?

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a highly asynchronous reinforcement learning pipeline with independent training and rollout generation workers. The system maintains stability by minimizing how off-policy the samples become, which is achieved through fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates. Inference workers can update weights mid-rollout, meaning later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy. Additionally, the system employs MoE routing replay to reduce divergence between the sampling and training policy.
questions.question: In Composer 2's asynchronous RL training, inference workers are capable of updating weights mid-rollout, meaning later tokens are less off-policy.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: For regularization in reinforcement learning, Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. While many open-source implementations use the k3 estimator, which becomes extremely high-variance when the policies diverge significantly, Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator instead. The k1 estimator is defined as -log r where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). This choice was made because the variance of the k3 estimator increases drastically as policies diverge, making it unsuitable for cases with large KL values.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use to avoid variance blow-up when policies diverge?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 uses the k1 estimator (-log r) because the k3 estimator, while unbiased, has variance that increases drastically as p and q diverge, making it unsuitable for cases with large KL values.

questions.lessonTitle: Precision Formats Used in Composer 2 Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses in-house kernels written in CUDA, PTX, and ThunderKittens/ParallelKittens to optimize low-precision training of the Mixture-of-Experts layer. The training recipe employs both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats. Composer 2 exclusively targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for block-scaled tensor-core matrix multiplications with in-hardware dequantization during systolic-array matrix multiplication. For the MoE forward pass, a novel variant of NVFP4 is used where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with a block size of 16 and FP32 per-token scales.
questions.question: What precision formats does Composer 2 training use?

questions.lessonTitle: RL Infrastructure Scales Across Multiple Regions
questions.lessonContent: The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. Our RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. A decoupled service stack enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. We use a fully asynchronous, high-throughput training stack built on Ray and PyTorch. The infrastructure supports fault-tolerant training down to the process or process-group level with both passive and active health checks.
questions.question: Composer 2's production training job spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (38.0%). In comparison, Opus 4.6 High achieves 58.2% and GPT-5.4 achieves 63.9%. On SWE-bench Multilingual, Composer 2 scores 73.7%, and on Terminal-Bench it achieves 61.7%. The CursorBench evaluation includes metrics beyond functional correctness, targeting code quality, execution efficiency, and interactive agent behavior.
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct CursorBench score for Composer 2?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, which is a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (44.2%) and 61% over Composer 1 (38.0%).

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation process for Composer 2 using CursorBench follows a structured workflow: First, the codebase environment is initialized for each task, providing the necessary context for agent interactions. Second, the task prompt is initialized with the specific problem to be solved. Third, the agent runs in the environment, executing actions just as it would in production. After the agent completes its rollout, accuracy metrics are computed to determine task success, and these results are aggregated over multiple passes to reduce variance. The process then involves measuring efficiency metrics like completion tokens and latency, before finally outputting the evaluation results.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (Claude will pull these in on demand), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all Claude sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: In which location can CLAUDE.md files NOT be placed according to the documentation?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety, requesting permission for any action that might modify your system including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: Select 'Always allow' when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code requests permission for actions that might modify your system: file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting information you want Claude to remember. The recommended content includes common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette such as branch naming and merge vs. rebase, developer environment setup like which compilers work, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. While there's no required format for CLAUDE.md files, the recommendation is to keep them concise and human-readable.
questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended type of content to include in a CLAUDE.md file?
questions.explanation: Code style guidelines are specifically recommended as appropriate content for CLAUDE.md files. The documentation lists code style guidelines along with common bash commands, testing instructions, and repository etiquette as suitable content for CLAUDE.md files. Personal shopping lists are not relevant to coding workflows and are not mentioned as recommended content.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Setting Up CLAUDE.md for Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code setup, the process begins by creating a CLAUDE.md file in your repository root or home folder, which Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. Once the file exists, you then add content to it documenting common bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and other information you want Claude to remember. After adding content, you should tune your CLAUDE.md files by experimenting with different instructions and determining what produces the best instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up CLAUDE.md for Claude Code?

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Claude Code's Test-Driven Development Workflow
questions.lessonContent: The test-driven development (TDD) workflow with Claude Code involves a specific sequence of steps designed to create verifiable, iterative code. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs while explicitly stating you're doing TDD so it avoids creating mock implementations for non-existent code. Second, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly instructing it not to write implementation code at this stage. Third, you ask Claude to commit the tests when satisfied. Fourth, you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests while instructing it not to modify the tests, telling it to keep iterating until all tests pass. The workflow leverages Claude's ability to make incremental improvements against a clear target provided by test cases.
questions.question: In the TDD workflow with Claude Code, at which step does Claude write the actual implementation code?
questions.answer: Step 4 - when asked to write code that passes the tests

questions.lessonTitle: Claude Code Supports Multiple Git Worktrees Simultaneously
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, enabling multiple Claude sessions to work on different parts of a project simultaneously. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. When using worktrees, you can have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a data visualization component, working at full speed without merge conflicts. The workflow involves creating worktrees with 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', then launching Claude in each worktree with different tasks. This approach is lighter-weight than having multiple full git checkouts.
questions.question: True or False: Git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog across all worktree directories.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag with a prompt, and the --output-format stream-json flag for streaming JSON output. However, headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each time you need it. This makes it suitable for automated workflows that run repeatedly but require reinitialization each session.
questions.question: Does headless mode in Claude Code persist between sessions?
questions.answer: No, it does not persist between sessions

questions.lessonContent: One effective multi-Claude workflow involves having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. This approach mirrors how multiple engineers collaborate, where having separate context can be beneficial. The process involves using one Claude to write code, then running /clear or starting a second Claude in another terminal, having the second Claude review the first Claude's work, and finally starting another Claude to read both the code and review feedback for editing. Claude instances can also communicate with each other by giving them separate working scratchpads and specifying which one should write to and which one should read from.
questions.question: True or False: One Claude can effectively review code written by another Claude in a separate session.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees vs Multiple Git Checkouts
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees offer a lighter-weight alternative to maintaining multiple git checkouts of your repository. While both approaches allow running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, there is a key difference in how they handle Git data. With git worktrees, each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files, but all worktrees share the same Git history and reflog across all worktree directories. This is different from having multiple separate git checkout folders, where each would have its own independent Git history.
questions.question: What is the key difference between using git worktrees versus having multiple separate git checkout folders for multi-Agent workflows?
choices: Git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog across all directories
Git worktrees cannot run Claude Code simultaneously
Git worktrees require separate git initialization for each directory
Git worktrees prevent merge conflicts between branches
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog across all worktree directories, while multiple separate git checkouts would each have independent Git histories.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. These color values follow a standard range where 0 represents the absence of a color and 255 represents its maximum intensity. For example, the RGB value rgb(255, 147, 41) represents a bright orange color. This three-channel system (RGB) is used to represent digital images, though some images also include a fourth channel called alpha for transparency.
questions.question: What is the numerical range for each color channel (red, green, blue) in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: At first glance, images appear smooth and continuous, much like what we see in the real world. However, when you magnify an image sufficiently, you discover that it is actually constructed from a grid of discrete colored squares called pixels. Each of these pixels contains specific numerical values rather than continuous color information. This fundamental understanding explains why image compression is necessary - computers must store or transmit millions of these individual pixel values to represent a complete image.
questions.question: True or false: When you zoom in far enough on a digital image, you will see that it is made of tiny colored squares called pixels.

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression is a method that preserves every single pixel of an original image while still reducing file size. The PNG file format is a common example that uses this approach, making it ideal for screenshots, graphics with text, and images requiring exact pixel reproduction. PNG achieves compression through multiple stages, wrapping the compressed data in a structured format organized into chunks. Each chunk serves a specific purpose, such as storing image metadata in the IHDR chunk or containing the actual compressed image data in the IDAT chunk.
questions.question: Which file format is an example of lossless compression that preserves every pixel while reducing file size?
questions.explanation: PNG (Portable Network Graphics) is explicitly mentioned in the content as a format that uses lossless compression to preserve every single pixel while still shrinking the file size. JPEG uses lossy compression, while MP3 is an audio format and GIF is another image format that also supports lossless compression but is not the primary example used in this content.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses lossless compression to preserve every pixel while shrinking the file. The process works in sequence: first, Filtering stores differences instead of actual pixel values to make data easier to compress. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding replaces repeated sequences with back-references to reduce redundancy. Third, Huffman Coding gives common values shorter binary codes to further reduce size. Finally, all the compressed data gets wrapped in the PNG format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression divides the image into uniform square blocks before processing. Each block contains exactly 8×8 pixels. These blocks are then transformed into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs contain mostly smooth gradients, most of the visual information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes typically won't notice, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: How many pixels are in each block that JPEG processes?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works to achieve much smaller file sizes. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, so JPEG reduces color resolution since you won't notice. The tradeoff is that once you apply lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back. The compression discards data that the algorithm determines won't be visually significant. This is fundamentally different from lossless compression, which preserves every single pixel perfectly.
questions.question: True or false: With lossy compression, you can recover the exact original pixels by decompressing the file.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression offers adjustable quality levels that control how much data gets discarded. At high quality settings, the compressed image closely resembles the original with minimal visible difference. As you increase compression (lower quality), more high-frequency details are discarded, which removes fine details like sharp edges and text. At very high compression levels, you will see blocking artifacts—visible square patterns where the 8×8 blocks become apparent. The compression ratio can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference at high quality.
questions.question: What happens to image quality as you increase the compression level in JPEG?
choices: Only the color information is affected, not the details
Fine details are lost and blocking artifacts become visible
The image becomes sharper and clearer
The file size stays the same but quality improves
questions.explanation: As JPEG compression increases, high-frequency details representing fine edges are discarded, and the 8×8 block structure becomes visible as blocking artifacts.

questions.lessonContent: In lossy compression like JPEG, the image is first divided into 8x8 pixel blocks. Each block is then transformed to frequency components using a mathematical transform. After that, the high-frequency components, which represent fine details, are discarded to achieve compression. This process exploits human vision's sensitivity to brightness over color. The result is a significantly smaller file size with minimal visible loss.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the JPEG lossy compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Prediction Methods for Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses four prediction methods to reduce file size by storing differences between adjacent pixels rather than storing each pixel value directly. The Sub method predicts each pixel will be the same as its left neighbor and stores only how wrong that guess was, which works best for horizontal gradients. The Up method predicts from the pixel above and works best for vertical gradients. The Average method predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. The Paeth method smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal pixels based on which is closest to the actual value. PNG encoders try each method for each row and automatically select the one that produces the best compression.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method works best for horizontal gradients?

questions.lessonTitle: LZ77 Sliding Window in Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: After the filtering step, PNG's compression algorithm looks for repeated patterns in the data using a method called LZ77. This algorithm maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data that it has already processed. When it finds a sequence that matches something within this window, instead of storing the full sequence again, it creates a back-reference that says 'go back X values and copy Y values.' This tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the entire sequence of values. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique helps reduce file size significantly.
questions.question: True or false: The LZ77 algorithm in PNG uses a sliding window of 32 KB to find repeated patterns.

questions.lessonTitle: Huffman Coding Bit Assignment in PNG Compression
questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding, some difference values appear much more frequently than others in PNG compression. Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more common values to save space. According to the content, the value 0 (representing no difference) appears 60% of the time and receives just 1 bit code. The value 2 appears 25% of the time and receives 2 bits. The value 255 appears 10% of the time and receives 3 bits. The value 127 appears only 5% of the time and also receives 3 bits. This approach works similarly to Morse code, where common letters like E get short codes while rare letters like Q get longer codes.
questions.question: In PNG's Huffman coding, which value receives a 1-bit code?
questions.explanation: The value 0 appears 60% of the time in filtered PNG data, making it the most common value, so it receives the shortest code of just 1 bit.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Roman Republic and Roman Empire Timeframes
questions.lessonContent: The Roman political history spanned two distinct periods. The first period was the Roman Republic, which lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. The second period was the Roman Empire, which lasted from 30 BCE to 476 CE. It is important to note that Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic as well, but the term Roman Empire specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period of unprecedented stability and prosperity. Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond during this time. Complete control meant there was almost no warfare within the empire. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, creating ideal conditions for trade, cultural exchange, and the extension of Roman citizenship to more and more provincials.
questions.question: The Pax Romana lasted nearly 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, meaning most high. In 23 BCE, Octavian was made consul for life and acquired several important titles. He was made Princeps, meaning first citizen, which became the origin of the word prince. He was also made Imperator, meaning successful general, which became the origin of the word emperor. Additionally, he was made Pontifex Maximus, meaning chief religious leader, which is the origin of the word pontiff used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: What title did Augustus receive that became the origin of the word prince?
questions.explanation: The title Princeps, meaning first citizen, was given to Augustus and is the origin of the word prince. This title was part of his effort to maintain the façade that he was an elected official rather than a dictator, as described in the concept of primus inter pares.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the title 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate, which solidified his political power and marked the beginning of the Roman Empire period.
questions.question: What is the correct order of Octavian's rise to power in establishing the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline, Division, and Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. In 285 CE, Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms - the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires. However, once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened significantly. The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer.
questions.question: Who divided the Roman Empire into two administrative realms, and when did this occur?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline, Division, and Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE. This division was intended to strengthen the empire through more effective administration. Once Constantine established Constantinople as the capital city, the division between east and west deepened considerably. The Western Roman Empire eventually ended in 476 CE, while the Eastern Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms because he believed it would weaken the empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline, Division, and Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Justinian was a powerful emperor of the Eastern (Byzantine) empire headquartered at Constantinople from 527-565 CE. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan who became a powerful co-ruler. Justinian managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last. His most significant accomplishment was rewriting Roman law into what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code, which still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today. The Plague of Justinian (541-542 CE), a bubonic plague, severely hurt the Byzantine empire.
questions.question: Which of the following was an accomplishment of Emperor Justinian?
choices: Rewrote Roman law into the Justinian Code
Established Christianity as the state religion
Conquered Jerusalem and destroyed the Second Temple
questions.explanation: Justinian rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code), which still forms the basis for civil law in several countries today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The End of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional end of ancient Rome as a political power in the West. Odoacer was a Germanic chieftain who overthrew the young emperor, though he initially claimed to rule on behalf of the Eastern emperor. The Western Empire had been declining for centuries through a combination of economic weakness, military problems, political instability, and social decline. The Eastern Empire, known as the Byzantine Empire, continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: When did the Western Roman Empire officially end, and who deposed the last emperor?
questions.answer: 476 CE when Romulus Augustus was deposed by Odoacer

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: Rome's Lasting Contributions to World History
questions.lessonContent: Ancient Rome is considered enormously important to world history for multiple reasons beyond just its territorial conquests. Rome made lasting contributions in administration of a vast empire, Christianity, architecture, engineering, historians, Jewish Diaspora, literature, Roman law, Romance languages, and transmission of Greek (Hellenistic) culture. The Romans were particularly skilled at adapting and improving upon ideas from other cultures, such as the Etruscan arch, which they used to build aqueducts. Roman law, particularly the Justinian Code, still forms the basis for civil law in several countries today. The Romance languages including French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish all developed from Latin.
questions.question: Ancient Rome is so important to world history only because of its military conquests and territorial expansion.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine played a crucial role in the transformation of Christianity from a persecuted sect to the dominant religion of the Roman Empire. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity, influencing his perspective on the faith. In 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration throughout the empire. This was a dramatic shift from the previous policy of persecuting Christians, as evidenced by Nero blaming them for the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE. Constantine eventually converted to Christianity on his deathbed. After the Western Roman Empire fell apart, the city of Rome became the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church, with the Pope using the imperial title "Pontiff".
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Constantine's relationship with Christianity?
choices: He founded Christianity as a new religion in Rome
He issued the Edict of Milan which legalized Christianity and later converted on his deathbed
He persecuted Christians throughout his entire reign
He banned all religions except Christianity
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE granted religious toleration to Christianity, legalizing it throughout the empire. Constantine later converted to Christianity on his deathbed, making him the first Christian Roman emperor.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. First, Galba became emperor following Nero's death. However, Galba was soon overthrown by his own general Otho, who then became emperor. This rapid succession of rulers illustrates the problems of imperial succession that plagued the Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. This architecture enables parallel processing where multiple subagents can work simultaneously on different aspects of a complex research question, with each subagent having its own context window for independent investigation.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does Anthropic's Research system use to coordinate multiple agents?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent research systems, token usage is the primary factor explaining performance variance. In the BrowseComp evaluation, token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other explanatory factors. Multi-agent architectures effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents. However, these systems burn through tokens quickly—in practice, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 is a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
questions.question: Token usage explains 80% of the performance variance in multi-agent research system evaluations.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations at Anthropic demonstrate that multi-agent research systems significantly outperform single-agent systems for breadth-first queries. A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches. This performance difference occurs because subagents can explore different aspects of a question simultaneously rather than sequentially.
questions.question: What was the percentage performance improvement of the multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents) over single-agent Claude Opus 4 on the internal research evaluation?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic discovered that Claude 4 models can function as excellent prompt engineers. When given a prompt and a failure mode, these models can diagnose why the agent is failing and suggest improvements. Anthropic created a specialized tool-testing agent that attempts to use flawed MCP tools, identifies the failures, and then rewrites the tool descriptions to prevent future failures. This agent tested each tool dozens of times, uncovering key nuances and bugs that were causing issues.
questions.question: What percentage decrease in task completion time did Anthropic achieve after the tool-testing agent rewrote tool descriptions?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic learned that agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so they embedded scaling rules directly into the prompts. For simple fact-finding tasks, the system uses just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls. Direct comparison tasks might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. Complex research tasks may use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries.
questions.question: A complex research task requiring independent investigation of multiple topics should use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating research outputs is difficult because they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times).
questions.question: Which three of the following are criteria used in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric?
choices: Factual accuracy, Citation accuracy, and Source quality
Citation accuracy, Completeness, and Response length
Factual accuracy, Response length, and Tool efficiency
Source quality, Tool efficiency, and Response length
questions.explanation: The five criteria are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Response length is not one of the criteria. Therefore, the first choice containing factual accuracy, citation accuracy, and source quality lists three of the actual criteria.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Effective evaluation of agents follows a sequential approach. First, we start evaluating immediately with small samples in early agent development since changes tend to have dramatic impacts. Then, LLM-as-judge evaluation scales when done well, using an LLM judge that evaluates each output against criteria in a rubric. After that, human evaluation catches what automation misses, finding edge cases that evals miss like hallucinated answers or subtle source selection biases. Finally, all these findings are used to refine prompts based on the evaluation results.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research system evaluation methodology?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Production Reliability and Engineering Challenges
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents. Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent code changes from breaking existing agents mid-process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Production Reliability and Engineering Challenges
questions.lessonContent: In traditional software, a bug might break a feature or cause outages. In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents, as restarts are expensive and frustrating for users.
questions.question: In agentic systems, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Production Reliability and Engineering Challenges
questions.lessonTitle: Engineering Challenges in Multi-Agent Production Systems
questions.lessonContent: Production multi-agent systems face unique engineering challenges. Currently, lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete before proceeding, which creates bottlenecks in information flow. Additionally, agents are stateful and errors compound over long-running processes. These challenges arise specifically from the stateful nature of agentic systems.
questions.question: Which of the following is a key engineering challenge specific to production multi-agent systems?
choices: Synchronous execution creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents
Lead agents execute subagents asynchronously by default
Agents are stateless and errors do not compound
Context windows are sufficient for all long-horizon conversations
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that synchronous execution creates bottlenecks. The content explicitly states that 'currently, our lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination, but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents.'

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. They are numerical representations that capture the semantic meaning of text in a vector space. Embeddings are used for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification. There has been increasing interest in retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models by finding relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and providing it to a generative model.
questions.question: Which application is NOT mentioned as a use case for text embeddings?

questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Capabilities of M2-BERT Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models with context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k. These M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. The long context capability means you can generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length options: 2k, 8k, and 32k.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is available at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms. This pricing advantage allows users to access powerful embedding models at a lower cost compared to alternatives. The platform offers 8 leading embedding models including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context.
questions.question: Which platform claims to be up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms for embeddings?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that Together Embeddings can be accessed at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.lessonTitle: Ordering Steps in Data Visualization with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: To visualize sample data from various domains using Together Embeddings, you first need to sample data examples and extract embeddings for each example using the sample_and_extract_embeddings function. Since embedding vectors have high dimensionality (768 for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K), you then need to transform the embedding vectors using tSNE to reduce them to 2D for visualization. Finally, you plot the transformed embedding vectors using the plot_embeddings function to display the visualization.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data visualization workflow using Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonTitle: Together Embeddings API Base URL Configuration
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have built applications using the OpenAI API to easily migrate their existing code. To configure the API, you need to set the base_url parameter to 'https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings' when initializing the OpenAI client. This enables seamless integration with existing workflows that were designed for OpenAI's embedding endpoints.
questions.question: What is the base_url required to configure the OpenAI client for the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI compatibility to simplify migration for developers. This compatibility means that applications already built using the OpenAI embeddings API can be easily switched to use Together's service by changing just the base URL and API key configuration. The code example demonstrates how to initialize the client with the Together API key and specify the base URL endpoint.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers to easily switch from OpenAI's embedding service.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integration with popular frameworks and vector databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation systems. According to the documentation, the platform offers integrations specifically with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG implementations. Additionally, users can also work with other vector databases such as Pinecone and Chroma when building RAG applications with the Together API.
questions.question: Which of the following frameworks IS mentioned as having a direct integration with Together Embeddings for building RAG?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that Together Embeddings has integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG. Among the options provided, LlamaIndex is mentioned as one of the frameworks with a direct integration. Pinecone, while mentioned in the documentation, is described as a vector database that can be used, not as a direct integration like the frameworks.

questions.lessonTitle: API Integration and Technical Setup: Function Definition and Execution
questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example using Together Embeddings, the technical implementation follows a specific sequence. First, the generate_embeddings function is defined to create embeddings from the Together API. Next, the sample_and_extract_embeddings function is defined to sample data and extract embeddings for each example. Finally, in the main script, the sample_and_extract_embeddings function is called with specific parameters including the data path, model API string, number of samples, and context length to retrieve the embedding vectors.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in defining and calling functions for the Together Embeddings API integration?

questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model produces embedding vectors with a dimension of 768, which is typically too large to easily visualize in its raw form. To plot each data example in two dimensions for visualization, the tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) technique is used to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional space suitable for plotting.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.lessonTitle: Vector Databases for RAG with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system is one of the most popular use cases for embedding models. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These vector databases store and retrieve embeddings efficiently, enabling semantic search capabilities that can be integrated with generative AI models.
questions.question: True or False: Pinecone is mentioned as a vector database option for building RAG with Together Embeddings.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization workflow using Together Embeddings follows a specific sequence. First, you define functions to extract samples from a data file and generate embeddings using the Together API. Then, you apply tSNE transformation to convert high-dimensional embeddings into lower dimensions suitable for plotting. Finally, you use matplotlib to create a scatter plot visualization showing how texts from different data sources cluster together based on their semantic similarities.
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence for data visualization with embeddings using Together?
choices: Transform with tSNE, generate embeddings, extract samples, create scatter plot
Generate embeddings, extract samples, create scatter plot, transform with tSNE
Extract samples, generate embeddings, transform with tSNE, create scatter plot
Create scatter plot, extract samples, transform with tSNE, generate embeddings
questions.explanation: The correct workflow starts with extracting data samples from files, then generates embeddings using the Together API, applies tSNE transformation to reduce dimensions, and finally creates a scatter plot visualization using matplotlib.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained in two distinct phases to develop its agentic software engineering capabilities. The first phase is continued pretraining, which improves the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding. The second phase is large-scale reinforcement learning, which improves end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. This two-phase approach allows the model to first build a strong coding knowledge foundation before refining its ability to solve complex, real-world software engineering tasks.
questions.question: What are the two training phases used for Composer 2?
questions.answer: Continued pretraining and large-scale reinforcement learning

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 continued pretraining stage uses Kimi K2.5 as its base model. This is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters. The model was selected based on internal evaluations measuring internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge through FreshBench, and state tracking capabilities. These evaluations led to the selection of Kimi K2.5 over other candidate models like DeepSeek V3.2 and GLM-5.
questions.question: Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three specific phases. The first phase spends the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length to build coding knowledge. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. The third phase is a short supervised fine-tuning phase on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to progressively specialize in coding capabilities while also extending its context handling ability.
questions.question: What are the three phases of continued pretraining in order?
choices: 32k token sequence length, long-context extension to 256k, and SFT on targeted coding tasks
Full sequence pretraining, short-context compression, and task-specific tuning
256k token sequence length, 32k context reduction, and SFT on general tasks
Initial coding training, intermediate context extension, and final RL fine-tuning
questions.explanation: The three phases are: 1) bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, 2) shorter long-context extension to 256k sequence length, and 3) short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining process for Composer 2 begins by selecting a base model, specifically Kimi K2.5, which was chosen based on evaluations of coding knowledge, state tracking, and codebase perplexity. The model then undergoes continued pretraining on code-dominated data, which is divided into three sequential phases: first spending the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks. After the main continued pretraining is complete, additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers are trained to enable faster inference through speculative decoding.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 continued pretraining process?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks that run in environments emulating real Cursor sessions. At a high level, RL training consists of three main steps: first, sampling a problem from the problem distribution; second, simulating a group of rollouts from the agent with different solutions; and third, updating the model weights based on solution quality. The problem distribution reflects the most common use cases, capturing many aspects of software engineering absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. In later stages of training, simple heuristics such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: What are the three steps of RL training in Composer 2 at a high level?
questions.answer: Sampling a problem, simulating a group of rollouts from the agent with different solutions, and updating the model weights based on solution quality

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline is built around learning from large-scale policy gradients while maintaining stability. The system operates in the single-epoch regime, meaning that the same prompt is never trained on twice throughout the entire training process. This approach ensures that each training example is used only once, preventing the model from overfitting to specific prompts and encouraging generalization. The policy gradient algorithm uses multiple samples per prompt with a fixed group size, allowing the model to explore different solution paths for each problem.
questions.question: Composer 2 trains using the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice.

questions.lessonTitle: Policy Gradient Algorithm Used in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 utilizes a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size for reinforcement learning training. This algorithm is operated in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. The system employs Adam as the underlying optimizer and updates the full parameter set during training. Following the approach in Dr. GRPO, the team found it crucial to minimize bias in the gradients that can arise from transforming the underlying advantage, which led them to remove the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces a length bias.
questions.question: Which policy gradient algorithm does Composer 2 use for reinforcement learning training?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 explicitly uses the GRPO algorithm, following the approach in Dr. GRPO where they remove the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces a length bias.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 was evaluated on CursorBench, an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. On CursorBench-3, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% accuracy, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (which achieved 44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (which achieved 38.0%). These evaluations were run directly within Anyrun, the same infrastructure that supports the reinforcement learning pipeline. In addition to accuracy, efficiency metrics like completion tokens, end-to-end latency, and inference cost were measured to ensure the model remains useful for interactive developer workflows.
questions.question: What accuracy score does Composer 2 achieve on CursorBench?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats for the Mixture-of-Experts layers. For the MoE forward pass, they use a variant of NVFP4 where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with block size 16 and FP32 per-token scales. For the MoE backward pass, they use the standard MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. This asymmetry is possible because on the forward pass, the trainer must match inference for numerical stability, while the backward pass runs only on the training cluster where higher precision improves training stability.
questions.question: In Composer 2 training, the MoE forward pass uses NVFP4 precision while the backward pass uses MXFP8 precision.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench was developed to address limitations in public evaluation benchmarks for coding agents. Public benchmarks like SWE-bench primarily focus on isolated bug-fixing, while Terminal-Bench covers wider task types but includes abstract puzzles. CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified with a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects real-world software engineering difficulty.
questions.question: Which benchmark has a higher median lines changed: CursorBench or SWE-bench Multilingual?
questions.explanation: CursorBench tasks have a median of 181 lines changed, compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, making CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations to customize how Claude behaves in different contexts. The first location is the root of your repo, or wherever you run claude from, which is the most common usage and can be checked into git to share with your team. The second location is any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos where you might run claude from subdirectories. The third location is any child of the directory where you run claude, where Claude will pull in CLAUDE.md files on demand when you work with files in those child directories. The fourth location is your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to all your claude sessions.
questions.question: In which four locations can you place CLAUDE.md files for Claude Code?
questions.answer: The root of your repo, any parent directory, any child directory, or your home folder

questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system: file writes, many bash commands, MCP tools, etc. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety while giving users flexibility to customize. There are four ways to manage allowed tools in Claude Code. First, you can select "Always allow" when prompted during a session.
