Second, you can use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist. Third, you can manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files. Fourth, you can use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: True or False: There are exactly four ways to manage allowed tools in Claude Code.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, allowing it to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) extends Claude's capabilities beyond its built-in features. There are three ways to configure MCP servers for use with Claude Code. First, you can configure MCP servers in project config, which makes them available when running Claude Code in that specific directory. Second, you can configure MCP servers in global config, making them available in all projects. Third, you can check in a .mcp.json file to your repository, which makes the MCP servers available to anyone working on your codebase. When working with MCP, it can be helpful to launch Claude with the --mcp-debug flag to help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: Which MCP configuration method makes tools available to anyone working on your codebase?
questions.explanation: A .mcp.json file that is checked into git makes MCP servers available to anyone working on your codebase, providing out-of-the-box functionality for all engineers in the project.

questions.lessonContent: To set up CLAUDE.md for customizing your Claude Code experience, you first need to create the CLAUDE.md file in your project or home directory. Once created, you must place the file in the appropriate location—either in the root of your repo, a parent or child directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. After the file is in place, you can tune the CLAUDE.md content by experimenting with instructions and refining what produces the best instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for setting up CLAUDE.md configuration files?
choices: Place in repo or home folder

questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands in Claude Code are stored as Markdown files in the .claude/commands folder and become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. These commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, a slash command file containing 'Please analyze and fix the GitHub issue: $ARGUMENTS.' can be invoked with /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to have Claude fix issue #1234. Custom commands can be checked into git to make them available to your team, and personal commands can be added to ~/.claude/commands for use across all sessions.
questions.question: What keyword enables custom slash commands to accept parameter values when invoked?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Headless mode is enabled using the -p flag with a prompt. The --output-format stream-json flag can be used to stream JSON output. Note that headless mode does not persist between sessions—you have to trigger it each session.
questions.question: True or False: Claude Code headless mode persists between sessions automatically.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers in three different ways to access their tools. Project config makes tools available only when running Claude Code in that specific directory. Global config makes tools available in all projects. A checked-in .mcp.json file makes tools available to anyone working on your codebase. For example, adding Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json means every engineer working on the repo can use these tools out of the box without individual configuration.
questions.question: Which MCP configuration method makes tools available to anyone working on your codebase?
questions.explanation: A checked-in .mcp.json file makes tools available to anyone working on your codebase because it is committed to source control and automatically loaded for all users.

questions.lessonTitle: Teaching Claude About Custom Bash Tools
questions.lessonContent: When introducing custom bash tools to Claude Code, you need to follow a specific sequence. First, tell Claude the tool name with usage examples so it understands what the tool does. Second, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation and learn about additional options. Third, document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md so Claude can reference them in future sessions. This systematic approach ensures Claude can effectively leverage your custom bash environment.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for teaching Claude about custom bash tools?
choices: Tell Claude the tool name with usage examples
Tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation
Document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag followed by your prompt. For streaming JSON output, which is useful for programmatic integration, you use the --output-format stream-json flag together. These flags allow Claude Code to work without user interaction, making it suitable for automated workflows and integration into larger processing pipelines.
questions.question: What two CLI flags are used together to enable headless mode with streaming JSON output in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code headless mode is designed for non-interactive contexts such as CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and various automation tasks. When using headless mode, each invocation runs independently without maintaining state from previous sessions. This means you must explicitly trigger headless mode each time you want to run a session, as it does not automatically persist between different invocations or remember previous interactions.
questions.question: True or False: Claude Code headless mode automatically persists between sessions.

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, Claude Code supports powerful applications involving multiple instances running in parallel. One effective approach is having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it, similar to working with multiple engineers. Another technique involves creating multiple git checkouts in separate folders and opening Claude in each with different tasks. A lighter-weight alternative uses git worktrees, which allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories while sharing the same Git history.
questions.question: Which multi-Claude workflow approach allows checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories while sharing Git history?
choices: Separate Claude instances for code writing and verification
Multiple git checkouts in separate folders
questions.explanation: Git worktrees enable checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, providing a lighter-weight alternative to multiple full checkouts while allowing parallel Claude sessions on different project tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The multi-Claude workflow for code review involves having one Claude instance write code while another reviews it with fresh perspective. First, you use Claude to write code for your task. Then you run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal to get separate context. Finally, the second Claude reviews the first Claude's work and provides feedback for improvement.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude code review workflow?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Digital images are composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. Each of these three color values can range from 0, which represents having none of that color, up to 255, which represents the maximum intensity of that color. With three color channels each ranging from 0-255, a single pixel requires 3 bytes of storage space to represent all its color information.
questions.question: What range of values can each of the three color channels (red, green, blue) have in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: A standard HD screenshot has dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, which calculates to exactly 2,073,600 total pixels. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage (one byte each for red, green, and blue), the raw image data would be 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, equaling 6,220,800 bytes. This translates to approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single uncompressed HD image. This large file size demonstrates why image compression techniques are essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently.
questions.question: A standard HD screenshot (1920 × 1080) contains 2,073,600 pixels, and each pixel needs 3 bytes. True or false: The raw, uncompressed file size would be approximately 6.2 megabytes.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses a three-step pipeline to achieve lossless compression while preserving every pixel perfectly. First, filtering stores differences between adjacent pixels rather than their actual values, because small difference numbers compress better. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references pointing to earlier occurrences. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, like zero, while giving longer codes to rare values. This specific sequence of filtering, then LZ77, then Huffman enables PNG to achieve 3x-50x compression without any loss of image quality.
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of techniques used in PNG lossless compression?
questions.explanation: PNG combines all three tricks in sequence: filtering stores differences first, then LZ77 replaces repeated patterns with references, and finally Huffman assigns shorter codes to common values.

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works to reduce file size without obvious quality loss. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. This is why JPEG reduces color resolution since your eyes won't detect the slight color variations.
questions.question: What aspect of human vision does lossy compression take advantage of: brightness resolution or color resolution?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: JPEG divides images into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. True or false

questions.lessonContent: When using lossy compression at high quality, the difference from the original is barely noticeable. However, when you crank up the compression setting, blocking artifacts appear where fine details get lost. The key trade-off is that with lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back. However, this trade-off is often worth it because files become 10-20x smaller with minimal visible difference.
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of lossy compression at high compression levels?
choices: Every single pixel can be perfectly recovered
Blocking artifacts appear where fine details are lost
Color resolution is increased beyond the original
The file size becomes larger than the original
questions.explanation: At high compression levels, JPEG produces blocking artifacts—visible block boundaries where fine details are lost. This is because the 8×8 block processing becomes apparent when high-frequency details are discarded.

questions.lessonContent: In JPEG lossy compression, after preparing the image data, the process moves to frequency analysis. First, the image is divided into 8x8 pixel blocks. Then, each block undergoes a mathematical transformation (DCT) that converts spatial data into frequency components. Finally, the compressor separates low-frequency components (smooth gradients) from high-frequency components (fine details) to determine which data can be discarded.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG's frequency analysis stage?

questions.lessonTitle: Lossless Compression Prediction Methods in PNG
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses four prediction methods to reduce file size by storing differences between pixels rather than absolute values. The 'Sub' method predicts each pixel from its left neighbor and works best for horizontal gradients. The 'Up' method predicts from the pixel above and is best for vertical gradients. The 'Average' method predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. The 'Paeth' method intelligently picks between left, above, or diagonal based on which is closest to the actual value. PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that compresses best for that specific row.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method works best for horizontal gradients: Sub, Up, Average, or Paeth?

questions.lessonTitle: LZ77 Sliding Window Size in PNG Compression
questions.lessonContent: After the filtering step, PNG uses an algorithm called LZ77 to find and replace repeated patterns with back-references. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data as it scans through the image. When it finds a pattern that has already appeared within this window, it references the previous occurrence instead of storing the data again. This is much more efficient than repeating values, because a small reference can replace a longer sequence of data. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data. True or false: Any pattern found within that window can be referenced instead of repeated, reducing file size.

questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression combines three main tricks in sequence: filtering to store differences, LZ77 to replace repeated patterns with references, and Huffman coding to give common values shorter binary codes. For a photograph, a 6.2 MB uncompressed image becomes approximately 2.1 MB after PNG compression, achieving about 3x smaller file size with zero quality loss. However, screenshots with large solid color regions can achieve much higher compression ratios, ranging from 10x to 50x smaller than the original file. This makes PNG particularly effective for computer screenshots and graphics with sharp edges rather than photographs.
questions.question: For which type of image does PNG achieve 10-50x compression: photographs, screenshots with solid colors, blurry images, or images with gradients?
questions.explanation: Screenshots with large solid color regions achieve 10-50x compression because the filtering and LZ77 steps can identify and eliminate highly repetitive pixel patterns.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three main techniques to compress image data while preserving every pixel. First, filtering predicts each pixel based on its neighbors and stores only the differences, which are typically small numbers. After filtering, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values and longer codes to rare ones. The final compressed data is then wrapped in the PNG file format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG's lossless compression pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Transformation from Republic to Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE. There were two periods of Roman government: the Roman Republic from 509 BCE-30 BCE, and the Roman Empire from 30 BCE-476 CE. Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, but the term "Roman Empire" specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors. This transition marked a fundamental shift in Roman governance from a republican system to an imperial system led by a single ruler with supreme authority.
questions.question: When did the Roman Empire officially begin according to the source content?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, resulting in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, creating unprecedented stability across the Roman world. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship, expanding the rights and privileges of people throughout the empire. The Pax Romana represented the height of Roman territorial expansion and political stability, with the empire reaching its greatest geographical extent under Emperor Trajan.
questions.question: The Pax Romana was a period of peace that lasted approximately 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, he was made consul for life and received several other titles including "Princeps" (meaning "first citizen," origin of the word "prince"), "Imperator" (meaning "successful general," origin of the word "emperor"), and "Pontifex Maximus" (meaning "chief religious leader," origin of the word "pontiff"). These titles collectively gave Augustus unprecedented power over the Roman state.
questions.question: Which of the following titles given to Augustus is the origin of the English word "emperor"?
questions.explanation: The title "Imperator" means "successful general" and is the origin of the English word "emperor."

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' Later, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now referred to as Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's transformation from victor to Augustus?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Power
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate and was also given several other titles. He was made "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which became the origin of the English word "prince." He also received the titles Imperator (origin of "emperor"), Pontifex Maximus (origin of "pontiff"), and tribune powers.
questions.question: What title was given to Augustus meaning "first citizen," which became the origin of the English word "prince"?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Power
questions.lessonContent: Augustus attempted to reform public morals by promoting family life, though this was largely unsuccessful. He began the practice of declaring emperors gods and of picking their own successors. He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure, including roads, and encouraged the growth of business. Augustus established fire and police departments for Rome and a strong money system. He extended citizenship to more and more provincials and is famously said to have "found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble." During his reign, Jesus, the founder of Christianity, was born in the Roman province of Judea.
questions.question: Augustus found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Power
questions.lessonTitle: Identifying the Emperor Who Built the Colosseum
questions.lessonContent: After the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE, Vespasian emerged as the new Roman emperor. He undertook major construction projects in Rome, most notably the building of the Colosseum. The Colosseum was a massive amphitheater where gladiatorial combats were held. Vespasian also oversaw the First Jewish Revolt, which resulted in the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE, carried out by his son Titus. Vespasian was succeeded by his son Titus, and then by his other son Domitian.
questions.question: Which Roman emperor built the Colosseum in Rome as a place where gladiatorial combats were held?
questions.explanation: Vespasian built the Colosseum in Rome as a place where gladiatorial combats were held. Nero was known for other buildings and infamous acts, Titus was Vespasian's son who completed the Colosseum after his father, and Trajan was known for Trajan's Column, Trajan's Forum, and Trajan's Market.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After Diocletian split the empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms, the Western Roman Empire faced numerous internal and external challenges. The Eastern Empire, also known as the Byzantine Empire, managed to survive much longer than its western counterpart. The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian leader named Odoacer. This event marked the traditional end of ancient Rome and the beginning of the Middle Ages in Western Europe.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end according to the source content?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine made one of the most significant decisions in Roman history when he moved the capital from Rome to the city of Byzantium. He renamed the city Constantinople, and today this city is known as Istanbul in modern Turkey. This move shifted the center of power from Rome to the East, ultimately contributing to the division between the Western and Eastern Roman Empires. The move was permanent and had lasting implications for the future of the Roman world.
questions.question: Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire made numerous lasting contributions to world civilization that continue to influence modern society. One of the most significant was the development of Roman law, which started with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and was later encapsulated in the Justinian Code in the 6th century CE. The Justinian Code still serves as the basis for civil law in many European countries today. Roman law established principles of public law (relationship of citizen to state), private civil law (relationships between people), and jus gentium (rights of foreigners).
questions.question: Which of the following Roman contributions to world history is correctly described as still being the basis for civil law in several countries today?
questions.explanation: The Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis) encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law development and remains the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Division and Administrative Split of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The process of dividing the Roman Empire began when Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE. This was the first step in creating what would become two separate empires. Later, Emperor Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming the city Constantinople. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened considerably.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative division of the Roman Empire?
choices: Constantine moves the capital from Rome to Byzantium (Constantinople)
Diocletian divides empire into east and west administrative realms

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The lead agent in this system is called the LeadResearcher, which enters an iterative research process. The LeadResearcher begins by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context, since if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated. The system creates specialized Subagents with specific research tasks, where each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the LeadResearcher.
questions.question: What is the name of the lead agent in Anthropic's Research system?

questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches. In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with token usage by itself explaining 80% of the variance.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems excel at breadth-first queries involving multiple independent directions.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation: token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice. Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance. However, there is a significant trade-off: in practice, these architectures burn through tokens very fast. In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 is a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
questions.question: According to the source, what percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation is explained by token usage alone?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other explanatory factors that together explain 95%.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Agent Effort to Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: When building multi-agent research systems, prompt engineering requires explicit guidelines for resource allocation. Anthropic found that agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so they embedded scaling rules in their prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions.
questions.question: According to the source, how many tool calls does a simple fact-finding query require?

questions.lessonTitle: Starting Search Strategy for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: Expert human researchers typically explore the landscape before drilling into specifics when beginning a new topic. Agents often default to overly long, specific queries that return few results, which is inefficient. Anthropic counteract this tendency by prompting agents to start with short, broad queries, evaluate what is available, then progressively narrow focus. This strategy mirrors how skilled humans approach research tasks.
questions.question: According to the source, agents should start their search with short, broad queries and then progressively narrow focus.

questions.lessonTitle: Tool Design Principles for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Tool design is critical in multi-agent systems because agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. Using the right tool is efficient and often strictly necessary. When agents encounter MCP servers with tools of varying quality, problems compound. Anthropic gave their agents explicit heuristics including: examine all available tools first, match tool usage to user intent, search the web for broad external exploration, and prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the heuristic that Anthropic explicitly recommended for tool selection?
choices: Prefer specialized tools over generic ones for better fit
Use only the first tool that appears in the list
Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Anthropic's agents were given the heuristic to 'prefer specialized tools over generic ones,' making this the correct answer. The other options are not mentioned in the source content - in fact, the source specifically recommends the opposite of generic tools.

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They therefore need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. They cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent code changes from breaking agents that might be anywhere in their process during deployment?

questions.lessonTitle: Synchronous Execution in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Currently, the lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination, but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: True or False: In Anthropic's Research system, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete before proceeding.

questions.lessonTitle: Evaluating Agents That Modify Persistent State
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations presents unique challenges. Unlike read-only research tasks, each action can change the environment for subsequent steps, creating dependencies that traditional evaluation methods struggle to handle. Anthropic found success focusing on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis. Instead of judging whether the agent followed a specific process, they evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state. For complex workflows, they break evaluation into discrete checkpoints where specific state changes should have occurred, rather than attempting to validate every intermediate step.
questions.question: What evaluation approach does Anthropic use for agents that modify persistent state across many turns?
choices: End-state evaluation - evaluating whether the agent achieved the correct final state rather than judging the process
Output-only validation - only checking the final output without considering state changes
Turn-by-turn analysis - validating every intermediate step the agent takes
Path compliance checking - ensuring agents follow prescribed steps exactly
questions.explanation: For agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations, Anthropic focuses on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis. They evaluate whether the agent achieved the correct final state instead of judging whether it followed a specific process, and break complex workflows into discrete checkpoints.

questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor system failures can be catastrophic because agents maintain state across many tool calls. To handle this, we first need to handle agent errors gracefully rather than restarting from the beginning, since restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Once errors are managed, we build systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards. Finally, adding full production tracing enables us to diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Production Reliability process for handling agent failures?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, offering 8 leading open-source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context (2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths). The platform provides state-of-the-art performance with comparable or better accuracies than closed models. Additionally, the M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Cost and Performance of Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings platform offers models at very competitive prices, being up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms. The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed to handle long documents while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. These models can process longer documents without requiring them to be split into many short chunks, which maintains more contextual information. The platform achieves state-of-the-art performance in MTEB benchmarks.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is more expensive than other popular embedding platforms.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint features full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate by changing the base URL and API key. The platform provides integrations with popular databases and frameworks including MongoDB, Pinecone, Chroma, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for building RAG systems. Users can access embedding models using specific API strings such as 'togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval' for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, which produces embedding vectors with a dimension of 768.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together API
questions.lessonTitle: Purpose and Function of RAG Systems
questions.lessonContent: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model. RAG systems combine the power of embedding-based retrieval with large language models to produce more accurate and contextually relevant outputs. This approach allows AI systems to access and utilize information that was not part of their original training data. The retrieval component uses semantic similarity to find the most relevant documents or passages from a knowledge base.
questions.question: What does Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) aim to overcome in generative AI models?
questions.answer: lack of knowledge from unseen data

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together API

The dimension of embedding vectors produced by this model is 768, which is the standard embedding size for this particular retrieval model. This high-dimensional embedding captures rich semantic information from the text, but it is too large to easily visualize in its raw form. To plot each data example in 2D for visualization purposes, a dimensionality reduction technique called tSNE is applied to transform these 768-dimensional vectors into a lower-dimensional space.

questions.lessonContent: When working with embeddings for data visualization, the high-dimensional nature of embedding vectors presents a challenge for plotting. The Together Embeddings documentation demonstrates how to address this by using tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform embedding vectors. In the provided visualization example, tSNE is applied with 2 components to reduce the 768-dimensional embeddings into a 2D space that can be easily plotted and interpreted. The transformation preserves the relative relationships between data points, allowing similar texts to appear close together in the visualization. This technique enables researchers to understand the structure and clustering of their data across different domains.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings visualization example uses tSNE to transform embedding vectors for 2D plotting.

questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embedding data using tSNE, specific parameters must be configured for optimal results. The Together Embeddings documentation provides a concrete example of how these parameters are set. In the data visualization pipeline, the transform_tSNE function accepts three key parameters: the embedding array, the number of components (set to 2 for 2D visualization), and the perplexity parameter. The perplexity parameter in the example is set to 15, which controls the balance between preserving local and global structure in the data. A perplexity of 15 is considered a moderate value that works well for datasets with around 50 samples as used in the RedPajama-v1 visualization example.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering, demonstrating strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. The model scores strongly on CursorBench, the researchers' benchmark of real-world software engineering, while also scoring at frontier levels on public benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch. The researchers develop infrastructure to support training in the same Cursor harness that is used by the deployed model, with equivalent tools and structure, and use environments that match real problems closely.
questions.question: What is the primary design purpose of Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained in two distinct phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance. The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding, which has long been demonstrated to drastically improve downstream performance. The researchers find that additional supervised learning reliably improves knowledge benchmarks and leads to improved coding performance of the final coding agent. For continued pretraining, they selected Kimi K2.5 as their base model, a 1.04T parameter with 32B active parameter Mixture-of-Experts model.
questions.question: Composer 2 is trained using a two-phase approach consisting of continued pretraining followed by large-scale reinforcement learning.

questions.lessonContent: Software engineering agents aim to autonomously act to solve a given task prompt, given an environment consisting of a codebase and an isolated container for code execution along with a prompt. An agent produces a rollout consisting of a series of actions, each of which makes one or more tool calls and yields responses. Tool calls may modify the underlying environment, and the result of a rollout is the final state of this environment. Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web. Its prompt includes a system message, the tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task.
questions.question: Which of the following describes a tool that Composer 2 has access to?
choices: Write new programming languages from scratch
Design user interfaces without external tools
Compile executables directly without using shell commands
questions.explanation: Composer 2 has access to tools for reading and editing files, running shell commands, and searching the codebase using grep or semantic search. The model does not directly compile executables - it uses shell commands to execute compilation through the terminal tool. Composer 2 is designed for software engineering tasks and does not include tools for creating new programming languages or designing user interfaces independently.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. The bulk of compute is spent at a 32k token sequence length, which provides the foundational coding knowledge improvement. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, there is a short supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase focused on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to first build strong base coding capabilities before extending its context window and then refining task-specific performance.
questions.question: What is the sequence length used during the bulk of continued pretraining compute in Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning training operates in a single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice. This approach differs from multi-epoch training where models see the same examples multiple times. In the context of RL for large language models, single-epoch training helps prevent overfitting to specific solution paths and encourages the model to explore diverse correct solutions rather than converging to a single approach.
questions.question: In Composer 2's reinforcement learning training, the same prompt is never trained on twice.

questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty for RL Reward
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward during RL training. The formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining curvature, and x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with few tool calls, every additional effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where agents might iterate for hundreds of tool calls. The penalty incentivizes the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing more thinking time on hard requests.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the nonlinear length penalty used in Composer 2's RL training?
choices: It is concave down and increasing, designed to encourage quick solutions on easy tasks while allowing more thinking on hard tasks
It is a linear penalty that equally weights all tokens regardless of task difficulty
It is a convex penalty that discourages thinking tokens in favor of immediate responses
It applies only to tool calling tokens and not to thinking or message tokens
questions.explanation: The correct answer describes the concave down and increasing nonlinear penalty, which is specifically designed to make the model efficient on easy tasks (few tool calls) while allowing more effort on hard tasks (many tool calls). The other options are incorrect because the penalty is explicitly nonlinear, not linear; it is concave down (not convex); and it applies to multiple token types including thinking, tool calling, tool output, and final message tokens.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. Second, a shorter long-context extension phase extends the model to handle 256k sequence length for processing larger codebases. Third, a brief supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase trains on targeted coding tasks to specialize the model for software engineering. These three phases must be completed in the correct chronological order to achieve the desired model capabilities.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the continued pretraining stage for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Because these tasks originate from real agent sessions rather than curated public repositories, CursorBench better reflects the true distribution of software engineering tasks while completely avoiding train-set contamination. According to Table 1, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (38.0%). This makes Composer 2 competitive with the strongest frontier models, achieving a score comparable to Opus 4.6 High (58.2%) and GPT-5.4 (63.9%).
questions.question: What accuracy does Composer 2 achieve on CursorBench?

questions.lessonTitle: CursorBench Task Complexity Compared to Public Benchmarks
questions.lessonContent: One of the key differences between CursorBench and public benchmarks lies in the structural characteristics of the tasks. CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are also more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: CursorBench tasks require an order of magnitude more code changes than public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. A decoupled service stack enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. The training service uses a fully asynchronous, high-throughput training stack built on Ray and PyTorch, with a centralized reconciler performing slot-based sample lifecycle state management. This design allows training to remain resilient to failures in other services, as evidenced by cases where partial or full outages in inference and environment infrastructure did not fail the training job.
questions.question: How many services make up the Composer 2 RL infrastructure architecture?
choices: Five (training, environments, inference, evaluations, and monitoring)
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Creating CLAUDE.md Files for Context Management
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, and developer environment setup. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (most common), any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of the directory, or your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md). When you name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git, you can share it across sessions and with your team. Alternatively, you can name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it for personal settings. The /init command automatically generates a CLAUDE.md for you when invoked.
questions.question: Where can you place CLAUDE.md files in your project hierarchy?
questions.answer: In the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of the directory, or your home folder (~/.claude/)

questions.lessonTitle: Tool Permission Management in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety, requesting permission for any action that might modify your system. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (we recommend checking the former into source control to share with your team), or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Managing Claude's Allowed Tools
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code requests permission for actions that might modify your system, including file writes and many bash commands. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools you know are safe or allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. The four methods to manage allowed tools include using the /permissions command to add tools like Edit for file edits or Bash(git commit:*) for git commits. You can also manually edit configuration files or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions. Without the gh CLI installed, Claude can still use the GitHub API or MCP server instead.

Changing the default model in settings.json

The file can be placed in the root of your repo, any parent or child of the directory where you run Claude, or your home folder. After choosing the file location, the next step is to Add content to CLAUDE.md with commands, code style guidelines, and workflow instructions. To teach Claude about your custom tools, you should tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md for future sessions.

MCP server connections can be configured in three ways: in project config for directory-specific availability, in global config for all projects, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file for team-wide availability.

questions.lessonContent: For repeated workflows like debugging loops or log analysis, you can store prompt templates in Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder. These become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. Commands in .claude/commands are available to your team when checked into git, while commands in ~/.claude/commands are personal and available in all sessions.

questions.lessonContent: A powerful multi-Claude workflow involves having one Claude instance write code while another verifies it. The workflow follows a specific sequence: First, use Claude to write initial code. Second, run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal to create separate context. Third, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work with fresh perspective. Fourth, start another Claude (or /clear again) to read both the code and review feedback. Fifth, have this final Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation of writing and reviewing often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude workflow where one Claude writes code and another verifies it?
questions.answer: Use Claude to write code; Run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal; Have the second Claude review the first Claude's work; Start another Claude to read both the code and review feedback; Have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files, enabling multiple Claude sessions to work simultaneously on different parts of a project. While each worktree maintains its own working directory, they share the same Git history and reflog, meaning commits and branches are accessible across all worktrees.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code headless mode (claude -p) integrates programmatically into larger workflows using two primary patterns. The first pattern called "fanning out" handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each task with specific tools. The second pattern called "pipelining" integrates Claude into existing data processing pipelines by calling claude -p with a prompt and piping the JSON output to the next processing step.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid pattern for using Claude Code headless mode with a custom harness?
choices: Sequencing runs Claude in sequence with human verification between each step
Fanning out handles large migrations by generating a task list and looping through individual Claude calls
Broadcasting sends identical prompts to multiple Claude instances simultaneously
Tunneling routes Claude traffic through a proxy for security
questions.explanation: Fanning out is explicitly described as a valid pattern where Claude writes a task list script and then loops through tasks calling Claude programmatically for each one.

questions.lessonContent: When using multiple Claude instances for code review, the process involves sequential steps where each Claude serves a specific role. First, you use Claude to write code. Then, you start a second Claude in another terminal to review the first Claude's work. Finally, you start a third Claude to read both the code and review feedback, enabling this third Claude to edit the code based on the feedback received.
