According to Anthropic's internal evaluations, a multi-agent system using Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. This test involved queries such as identifying all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, where the multi-agent system succeeded by decomposing the task into parallel subtasks for subagents while the single-agent system failed with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: By what percentage did the multi-agent system outperform single-agent Claude Opus 4 on the internal research evaluation?

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Comparison Between System Types
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than single-agent chat interactions. Anthropic's data shows that agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, while multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token consumption is a known downside of multi-agent architectures, making them most suitable for tasks where the value is high enough to justify the increased computational cost.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use approximately 15 times more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonTitle: Key Evaluation Criteria for Research Agent Outputs
questions.lessonContent: When evaluating research agent outputs, Anthropic uses an LLM-as-judge approach with multiple criteria. The evaluation rubric assesses factual accuracy by checking if claims match sources, citation accuracy by verifying that cited sources support the claims, completeness by ensuring all requested aspects are covered, source quality by preferring primary sources over lower-quality secondary ones, and tool efficiency by evaluating whether the right tools were used a reasonable number of times. This comprehensive rubric allows for scalable evaluation of hundreds of outputs.
questions.question: Which of the following criteria is used in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric for research agent outputs?
questions.explanation: The five criteria used are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Citation accuracy is one of these five criteria, while Response creativity, Source popularity, and Search efficiency are not part of the evaluation rubric.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic discovered that Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers. When given a prompt and a failure mode, these models can diagnose why the agent is failing and suggest improvements. They even created a tool-testing agent that attempts to use flawed MCP tools, identifies the issues, and then rewrites the tool descriptions to prevent failures. By testing the tool dozens of times, this agent found key nuances and bugs. This process for improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new descriptions.
questions.question: What percentage decrease in task completion time resulted from the tool-testing agent's improved tool descriptions?

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic found that traditional evaluations often assume AI follows the same steps each time, but multi-agent systems don't work this way. Even with identical starting points, agents might take completely different valid paths to reach their goal. One agent might search three sources while another searches ten, or they might use different tools to find the same answer. Because the correct steps aren't always known in advance, flexible evaluation methods are needed that judge whether agents achieved the right outcomes while also following a reasonable process.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems always follow the same predetermined path to reach their solution, making traditional step-by-step evaluation methods effective for assessing their performance.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Based on Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic embedded scaling rules in their prompts to help agents judge appropriate effort for different tasks. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls. Direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. Complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of their system.
questions.question: According to the scaling rules embedded in Anthropic's prompts, how many subagents should be used for direct comparison tasks?
choices: More than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, distinguishing this from simple fact-finding (1 agent) and complex research (more than 10 subagents).

questions.lessonContent: When evaluating multi-agent research systems, the process begins with testing a small set of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns to quickly identify dramatic impacts from changes. After establishing this initial sample, the next step involves defining rubric criteria that the LLM judge will use to evaluate outputs, including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Once the rubric is in place, the LLM judge scores each output against these criteria, providing a consistent evaluation method that scales effectively.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the prompt engineering and evaluation workflow for multi-agent research systems?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process. Code changes that seem well-meaning can break existing agents if they are updated all at once to a new version. Instead of simultaneous updates, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment technique does Anthropic use to prevent code updates from breaking agents that are currently running?

questions.lessonContent: Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors compound and minor system failures can become catastrophic. When errors occur in agentic systems, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Instead of restarts, Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, combining the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: In production agent systems, when errors occur during long-running tasks, restarting from the beginning is the most effective approach.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Management Strategies for Extended Conversations
questions.lessonContent: Production agents often engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management as standard context windows become insufficient. When context limits approach during long-horizon conversations, Anthropic implements patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. Agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs, and they can retrieve stored context like research plans from memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit.
questions.question: What strategy does Anthropic use when context limits approach during long-horizon conversations with hundreds of turns?
choices: Agents automatically compress all previous messages into a single summary
Agents pause and wait for the user to manually clear previous context
Agents terminate the conversation and start a new one
Agents summarize completed work and store essential information in external memory, then spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts
questions.explanation: When context limits approach, Anthropic's agents summarize completed work phases, store essential information in external memory, and spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs and retrieval of stored context.

questions.lessonTitle: Error Handling and Recovery in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: When errors occur in multi-agent systems, we cannot simply restart from the beginning since restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, we built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. We also use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully: for instance, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt works surprisingly well. We combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the error handling and recovery process for multi-agent systems?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, and offers 8 leading embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with options of 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The endpoint provides state-of-the-art performance in MTEB showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models from companies like OpenAI and Cohere.
questions.question: How many leading embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Capabilities of M2-BERT Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes M2-BERT retrieval models designed specifically for long context applications. These models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while maintaining more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: The M2-BERT retrieval models in the Together Embeddings endpoint support context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens.

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a mathematical measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. This fundamental capability enables various downstream applications including clustering similar documents together, performing semantic search to find related content, and classifying text into predefined categories. Additionally, text embeddings serve as the core component in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, which aim to overcome limitations of generative AI models such as lack of knowledge from unseen data by finding relevant information from a knowledge base.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide as a measure of?
choices: Similarity or relatedness of text queries
Number of tokens in a query
questions.explanation: Text embeddings explicitly provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries, which is their primary function as stated in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together. To integrate with Together, you configure the OpenAI client with a specific base URL pointing to Together's API infrastructure. The base URL for the Together Embeddings endpoint is https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings. You also need to provide your Together API key when initializing the client. This compatibility significantly reduces migration effort for existing applications.
questions.question: What is the base URL for the Together Embeddings endpoint API?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint has been designed with full OpenAI compatibility to facilitate easy migration for developers. This means that if you have already built applications using the OpenAI embeddings API, you can switch to the Together endpoint with minimal code changes. The compatibility applies to the entire API structure, including request and response formats. This design decision was made specifically to make migrating existing applications easier.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing easy migration of existing applications.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers embedding models at very competitive prices compared to other popular platforms. According to the documentation, you can access these powerful embedding models at prices that are up to 4x cheaper than other platforms. This cost advantage applies to all models available on the platform, including the state-of-the-art M2-BERT retrieval models. The pricing graph referenced in the documentation illustrates these cost differences, making Together an economical choice for developers building AI applications at scale.
questions.question: According to the documentation, how much cheaper are Together Embeddings compared to other popular platforms?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that you can access these powerful models at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.lessonTitle: API Integration and Setup - Embedding Request Flow
questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint with OpenAI API compatibility, you first need to import the OpenAI client library to access the necessary classes. Next, you must set the API key and base URL to configure authentication with the Together API endpoint. Finally, you create an embedding request using the client by specifying the input text and model, then extract the embedding vector from the response data.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps when setting up the Together Embeddings API client and making an embedding request?
choices: Set API Key and Base URL

questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize in a 2D plot. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768, which is too high-dimensional for direct visualization. To plot each data example in 2D, the documentation uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the embedding vectors from their high-dimensional space down to a lower-dimensional representation that can be plotted on a chart.
questions.question: What technique is used to transform embedding vectors for 2D visualization?

questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings from different data sources using the Together Embeddings endpoint and tSNE, the resulting plot shows how texts from each data source are grouped. The documentation shows an example using RedPajama-v1 sample data from multiple sources including arxiv, book, c4, github, and stackexchange. According to the documentation (page 7/8), 'texts from each data source are somewhat closely located.' The documentation also notes 'the similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are less related.' This indicates the clusters are near each other but not completely separate.
questions.question: True or False: According to the documentation, the t-SNE visualization shows texts from each data source appearing in separate, distinct clusters.

questions.lessonTitle: Integration Options for Building RAG Systems
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embedding models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integration with popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, developers can leverage frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex to build RAG systems using the Together API. These integrations allow developers to create powerful AI applications that can overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model.
questions.question: Which frameworks are specifically mentioned as integration options for building RAG systems with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that you can build RAG using Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma or by leveraging frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is built upon Kimi K2.5 as its base model, which is a 1.04 trillion parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 32 billion active parameters. This base model was selected after evaluating several open-source models including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2 using internal benchmarks measuring coding knowledge, state tracking capabilities, and codebase perplexity. Kimi K2.5 demonstrated strong performance with 83.2% on FreshBench for coding knowledge and was chosen for its general strong performance along with infrastructure efficiency considerations.
questions.question: What is the name and parameter count of the base model used for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases designed to progressively specialize the model on coding knowledge. The bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding capabilities. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that expands the context window to 256k tokens. Finally, a short supervised fine-tuning phase focuses on targeted coding tasks. During training, the evaluation loss on internal codebase decreases log-linearly over the course of the training run.
questions.question: Composer 2's continued pretraining is divided into three phases with the bulk of compute spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a long-context extension to 256k tokens, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks. True or false?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 introduces several key innovations in its training infrastructure to enable efficient scaling. Instead of the original MoE design that coupled Expert Parallelism (EP) with Tensor Parallelism (TP), Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than TP and improves compute efficiency. The training uses EP=8 and CP=2 for continued pretraining, and EP=8 and CP=8 for the reinforcement learning phase. The system also employs custom kernels written in CUDA, PTX, and ThunderKittens for optimizing low-precision training of the MoE layer using MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs.
questions.question: Which parallelism approach does Composer 2 use as its primary long-context scaling axis?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis because it requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. The benchmark addresses limitations of public benchmarks including domain mismatch, prompt over-specification, data contamination, and narrow evaluation scope. Compared to public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified with a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks.
questions.question: In CursorBench, what is the median number of lines changed per task?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. The system uses fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, similar to PipelineRL, which allows inference workers to update weights mid-rollout. This means later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy. To reduce divergence between sampling and training policy, the system replays MoE routing. The training employs a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and operates in the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice.
questions.question: Composer 2 uses asynchronous RL training where inference workers can update weights mid-rollout.

questions.lessonTitle: Policy Gradient Algorithm and KL Regularization
questions.lessonContent: For reinforcement learning regularization, Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler divergence KL(q||p) = Ex∼q[−log r(x)] where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source implementations estimate KL using the k3 estimator, which is unbiased but has variance that increases drastically as p and q diverge. The document notes that for large KL values, the variance of the k3 estimate is extremely large. Therefore, Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator = -log r instead. The training also removes the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces length bias, and does not normalize group advantages by their standard deviation.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use for RL regularization?
questions.explanation: The document explicitly states that Composer 2 uses the standard k1 = -log r instead of k3 because k3 has variance that increases drastically as p and q diverge, making it unsuitable for large KL values.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline operates through a sequence of key steps. First, a problem is sampled from the training distribution. Then, the agent generates multiple rollouts by exploring different solutions to that problem. Finally, these solutions are evaluated to determine their quality and correctness.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% accuracy on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (which achieved 44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (which achieved 38.0%). These accuracy metrics are computed by running Cursor agents directly within Anyrun, the same infrastructure that supports the reinforcement learning pipeline. For each task in CursorBench, the codebase environment is initialized along with the initial task prompt, and the agent executes exactly as it would in the production environment.
questions.question: What is the accuracy score of Composer 2 on CursorBench?

questions.lessonContent: Inference workers in Composer 2's RL training infrastructure are capable of updating weights mid-rollout, meaning that later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy. This is achieved through fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, similar to PipelineRL. This capability helps minimize divergence between the sampling and training policy, which is particularly important since agent rollouts can be very long when aiming for long-horizon coherency. To further reduce divergence between sampling and training policy, the system also replays MoE routing.
questions.question: In Composer 2's asynchronous RL training infrastructure, inference workers can update weights mid-rollout to reduce policy divergence. True or false?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses different parallelism configurations for its continued pretraining and reinforcement learning phases. For continued pretraining, the configuration uses EP=8 and CP=2. For the reinforcement learning phase, the configuration shifts to EP=8 and CP=8, which allows for larger expert-parallel degrees and more efficient expert-grouped GEMMs with larger per-rank token batches. DeepEP is used to implement high-throughput token dispatch and combine for the expert parallelism.
questions.question: What parallelism configuration does Composer 2 use for the RL phase?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that Composer 2 uses EP=8, CP=2 for continued pretraining and EP=8, CP=8 for the RL phase.

questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's asynchronous RL training, weight synchronization from training to inference workers follows a specific pipeline. First, the training process generates weight updates at each training step. To minimize transfer size, these updates undergo delta compression where each rank caches its previous upload and transmits only the diff against the new weights. The compressed updates are then uploaded to a shared S3 bucket, with uploading fully sharded across all training ranks to saturate egress bandwidth. Each inference cluster independently downloads and reconstructs weights from the shared delta chain, requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Composer 2's weight synchronization from training to inference?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Customizing Your Setup and Adding Tools
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repository (the most common usage), which you can name CLAUDE.md and check into git to share across sessions and with your team, or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md files in any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos, or in any child of the directory where you run claude. Additionally, you can place a CLAUDE.md file in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies it to all your claude sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: Where is the recommended location to place a CLAUDE.md file if you want to share it across sessions and with your team?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Customizing Your Setup and Adding Tools
questions.lessonContent: Your CLAUDE.md files become part of Claude's prompts, so they should be refined like any frequently used prompt. A common mistake is adding extensive content without iterating on its effectiveness. At Anthropic, they occasionally run CLAUDE.md files through the prompt improver and often tune instructions by adding emphasis with 'IMPORTANT' or 'YOU MUST' to improve adherence. You can add content to your CLAUDE.md manually or press the # key to give Claude an instruction that it will automatically incorporate into the relevant CLAUDE.md.
questions.question: CLAUDE.md files become part of Claude's prompts and should be refined like any frequently used prompt.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Customizing Your Setup and Adding Tools
questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system: file writes, many bash commands, MCP tools, etc. We designed Claude Code with this deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: Select 'Always allow' when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following is a method for managing allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Using the /config command to add or remove tools from the allowlist
Selecting 'Always allow' when prompted during a session
Using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Always allow' because it is one of the four methods stated in the source content. The other options are either not mentioned (/config) or are also valid methods, but only one answer can be selected.

questions.lessonContent: When working with Claude Code, you can use specific phrases to trigger different levels of thinking budget. The system maps these phrases directly to increasing levels of computation time: "think" provides the smallest budget, followed by "think hard", then "think harder", and finally "ultrathink" which allocates the most thinking budget. This extended thinking mode gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly before responding. Using these specific phrases is particularly useful when asking Claude to plan solutions for complex problems that require deeper analysis.
questions.question: What is the correct order of thinking budget levels from lowest to highest in Claude Code?
questions.answer: think, think hard, think harder, ultrathink

questions.lessonContent: The /clear command in Claude Code is used to reset the context window during long sessions. When Claude's context window fills with irrelevant conversation, file contents, and commands, this can reduce performance and sometimes distract Claude from the main task. Using /clear frequently between tasks helps keep context focused and maintains optimal performance throughout the session.
questions.question: The /clear command in Claude Code should be used to keep context focused during long sessions.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports multiple methods for providing visual inputs to help with development tasks. One method involves using a keyboard shortcut on macOS where you press cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot directly to clipboard, then ctrl+v to paste into Claude. Another method allows you to drag and drop images directly into the prompt input. Additionally, you can provide file paths for images so Claude can read and analyze them. These visual capabilities are particularly useful when working with design mocks as reference points for UI development, and for analyzing visual charts during debugging.
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct macOS keyboard shortcut to screenshot to clipboard for use with Claude Code?
questions.explanation: The correct shortcut is cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot directly to clipboard, then ctrl+v to paste into Claude. This is different from the standard macOS screenshot shortcut (cmd+shift+4).

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Claude Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag followed by your prompt. For streaming JSON output, you can use the --output-format stream-json flag. It's important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions—you have to trigger it each session you want to run Claude non-interactively. This mode allows Claude Code to be integrated programmatically into larger automation workflows.
questions.question: What flag is used to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Claude Strategies
questions.lessonContent: A powerful multi-Claude strategy involves having one Claude write code while another Claude verifies or tests it. The workflow typically follows these steps: first use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal. The second Claude then reviews the first Claude's work. After that, you start another Claude (or /clear again) to read both the code and review feedback, and have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything. Claude instances can communicate by giving them separate working scratchpads and telling them which one to write to and which one to read from.
questions.question: In a multi-Claude verification workflow, after the second Claude reviews the first Claude's work, the next step is to start another Claude (or /clear again) to read both the code and review feedback.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Claude Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts. The basic commands are: git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a to create a worktree, then cd ../project-feature-a && claude to launch Claude in that worktree.
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using git worktrees for running multiple Claude instances compared to multiple git checkouts?
choices: Git worktrees provide faster network access to GitHub
Git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog, making them lighter-weight than full checkouts
Git worktrees require fewer terminal tabs to manage
Git worktrees automatically create new branches for each task
questions.explanation: Git worktrees are lighter-weight because they share the same Git history and reflog while each having isolated working directories, unlike full git checkouts which duplicate the entire repository history.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Claude Strategies
questions.lessonContent: In the multi-Claude workflow for code review and editing, the process begins with the first Claude writing the initial code. Then a second Claude instance is started to review the code that was written by the first Claude. Finally, the code is edited based on the review feedback provided by the second Claude. This sequential process leverages multiple Claude instances to improve code quality through independent review.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude code review and editing workflow?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images are made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that pixel's color. Each of these three color values can range from 0, representing none of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. For example, the orange color rgb(255, 147, 41) contains maximum red (255), medium green (147), and low blue (41). A full HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel needs 3 bytes (one for each RGB channel), an uncompressed HD image would be approximately 6.2 megabytes.
questions.question: What is the range of possible values for each color channel (red, green, or blue) in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression is one of the two main approaches to image compression, with lossy compression being the other. Lossless compression preserves every single pixel of the original image while still reducing the file size. It uses clever techniques to store pixel data more efficiently without throwing away any information. This means when you decompress a losslessly compressed image, you get exactly the original pixel values back. PNG is a common format that uses lossless compression, making it ideal for screenshots, graphics with text, and images where exact pixel reproduction is critical.
questions.question: Lossless compression removes data that humans won't notice, similar to how JPEG works.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG is a lossy compression format that exploits characteristics of human vision to reduce file size. The human eye resolves brightness in fine detail but blurs colors together, meaning we notice sharp edges but not slight color variations. JPEG takes advantage of this by first converting pixels from RGB to a different color format that separates brightness from color. It then reduces color resolution since our eyes won't notice. Finally, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges.
questions.question: What is the size of the pixel blocks that JPEG divides the image into for processing?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that JPEG 'divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.' The other options (4×4, 16×16, 32×32) are not mentioned in the source material.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonTitle: Human Vision and Color Resolution in JPEG
questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits specific characteristics of human vision. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. This is because the human visual system processes luminance (brightness) with much higher spatial resolution than chrominance (color). JPEG takes advantage of this by first converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice the difference.
questions.question: What aspect of human vision does JPEG primarily exploit when reducing color resolution?
questions.answer: Human eyes blur color together but resolve brightness in fine detail

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: Once JPEG compression is applied, the original pixel data cannot be fully recovered. JPEG throws away high-frequency details that the human visual system typically won't miss, such as fine edges and subtle color variations. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components, and the discarded high-frequency data is permanently lost. While at high quality settings the difference may be barely noticeable, the compression is irreversible.
questions.question: After applying JPEG compression, is it possible to recover the exact original pixel data?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: JPEG processes images by dividing them into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforming each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients and gradual color transitions found in photographs. High frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges and texture. Since natural photographs consist mostly of smooth gradients, most of the visual information can be captured in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG strategically discards high-frequency data while preserving low-frequency data, achieving significant file size reduction.
questions.question: In JPEG compression, which type of frequency component represents fine details like sharp edges?
questions.explanation: High-frequency components represent fine details like sharp edges, while low-frequency components represent smooth gradients. JPEG discards high-frequency data since human eyes cannot perceive fine detail as well as smooth gradients.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses prediction (filtering) to compress images by storing how each pixel differs from its neighbor instead of storing the absolute value. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub predicts from the left neighbor and works best for horizontal gradients, Up predicts from the pixel above and works best for vertical gradients, Average predicts from the average of left and above pixels, and Paeth smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal based on which is closest. PNG encoders try each method per row and automatically select the one that compresses best for that particular row of data.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method intelligently selects between left, above, or diagonal neighbors?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: After prediction, PNG uses the LZ77 algorithm to find repeated patterns in the data. LZ77 scans through the data looking for sequences that have appeared before within a recent window. When it finds a repeat, instead of storing the same sequence twice, it creates a back-reference that says "go back X values and copy Y values." This reference is much smaller than repeating the actual values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data to find repeating patterns.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG combines three main compression tricks in sequence to shrink image files while preserving all pixel data. First, filtering stores differences between pixels rather than absolute values, making the data more compressible. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently. The final step wraps everything in the PNG file format with headers and checksums. For a photograph, this achieves approximately 3x compression with zero quality loss.
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of techniques used in PNG compression?
choices: Huffman, Filtering, LZ77, then wrap in PNG format
Filtering, LZ77, Huffman, then wrap in PNG format
LZ77, Filtering, Huffman, then wrap in PNG format
Huffman, LZ77, Filtering, then wrap in PNG format
questions.explanation: PNG applies filtering first to predict and store differences, then uses LZ77 to find repeated patterns, followed by Huffman coding to assign shorter codes to common values, and finally wraps everything in the PNG file format.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three main tricks to compress images while preserving every pixel perfectly. First, filtering predicts each pixel based on its neighbors and stores only the differences, which are usually small numbers. Next, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in these differences and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman encoding gives common values like 0 shorter binary codes while using longer codes for rare values.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three core compression techniques used in PNG lossless compression?

questions.moduleTitle: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire began after Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, making him the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also given the titles "Princeps" (meaning "first citizen," which is the origin of the word "prince") and "Imperator" (meaning "successful general," which is the origin of the word "emperor"). Augustus maintained the façade that he was an elected official rather than a dictator through the Latin phrase primus inter pares, meaning "first among equals," suggesting he was the most prestigious senator while others remained equal.
questions.question: In what year was Augustus made consul for life by the Senate?

questions.moduleTitle: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Augustus's Reign and the Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: Augustus transformed Rome during his reign, claiming he "found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble." He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure, including roads, and established fire and police departments for Rome. The Pax Romana was a period of nearly 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region with almost no warfare. During this golden age, Augustus extended citizenship to more and more provincials, and Jesus, the founder of Christianity, was born in the Roman province of Judea during his reign.
questions.question: The Pax Romana was a period of peace that lasted for approximately 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After Augustus died, several emperors followed him with varying levels of capability and success. Tiberius (14-37 CE) was Augustus's stepson and a capable general who extended the empire's northern frontier and strengthened the empire. Caligula (37-41 CE) earned his nickname "little boots" from the Roman army as a child and began with two years of effective rule before his rule became horrible, resulting in him being assassinated by the Praetorian Guard. Claudius (41-54 CE) brought southern Britannia under Roman control and opened the Senate to provincials, becoming emperor because he was the last adult male of his family.
questions.question: Which emperor brought southern Britannia (what later became Great Britain) under Roman control?
questions.explanation: Claudius (41-54 CE) brought southern Britannia under Roman control, as well as several kingdoms in the East. Caligula ruled for only 4 years (37-41 CE), Tiberius was Augustus's stepson and ruled from 14-37 CE, and Nero ruled from 54-68 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian leader named Odoacer. This event marked the end of the ancient Roman Empire in the West after nearly 500 years of imperial rule beginning with Augustus in 30 BCE. The Eastern Byzantine Empire, however, continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The Western Empire had been weakening for centuries due to various economic, military, political, and social problems that accumulated over time.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian and the Crisis of the Third Century
questions.lessonContent: Following the death of Marcus Aurelius, Rome experienced a century of chaos known as the Crisis of the Third Century. During this period, the empire faced civil wars, economic collapse, barbarian invasions, and rapid changes in imperial leadership. Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence. He was an absolute ruler who ended all personal liberties and divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE, which was the first step toward creating two separate empires.
questions.question: Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to restore order after the Crisis of the Third Century.

questions.moduleTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine moved the capital of the Roman Empire from Rome to Byzantium in 312-337 CE. He renamed the city Constantinople, which today is known as Istanbul in modern Turkey. This move permanently shifted the center of power from Rome to the East. Constantine also enacted the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration throughout the empire. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity, and Constantine himself converted to Christianity on his deathbed.
questions.question: Which emperor moved the capital from Rome to Constantinople?
questions.explanation: Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople. This was a pivotal moment that deepened the split between the Eastern and Western empires.

questions.moduleTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Decline and Fall of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The division of the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western halves was a gradual process that ultimately led to the fall of the Western Empire. Emperor Diocletian first divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, creating separate East-West administration. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople, establishing it as the Eastern capital. These actions deepened the East-West split, with the Western Empire ending in 476 CE and the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasting until 1453 CE.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the division of the Roman Empire and establishment of Constantinople as the Eastern capital?

questions.lessonTitle: Roman Law and the Justinian Code
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. The law was divided into public law (relationship of citizen to state), private or civil law (relationships between people), and peoples law (jus gentium, rights of foreigners). Emperor Justinian in the 6th century CE encapsulated the previous 1000+ years of Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, also known as the Justinian Code. This code is still used as the basis of civil law in many parts of Europe today.
questions.question: What was the name of the legal code compiled by Emperor Justinian that encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law?

questions.lessonTitle: Christianity's Spread Through the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Christianity started in the Roman province of Judea. The Pax Romana and Roman infrastructure allowed early Christians, as citizens of the Roman Empire, to travel freely throughout the empire. There was a significant number of Christians in Rome by 64 CE, the year Nero blamed them for the fire. According to tradition, Paul of Tarsus used his Roman citizenship to have his criminal trial relocated to Rome from Caesarea in the 60s CE. Christianity finally gained acceptance with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE and Constantine's conversion on his deathbed.
questions.question: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE granted religious toleration and legalized Christianity in the Roman Empire.

questions.lessonContent: Romance languages developed from Latin and include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. Old English was a Germanic language, but William the Conqueror of Normandy brought French (a Romance language) to England in 1066. Middle English, the forerunner of modern English, is a mixture of these old Germanic and French languages. About half of modern English can be traced to Latin. Additionally, the Catholic Church preserved the Latin language, and Catholic masses were said in Latin until the 1960s.
questions.question: Which of the following languages belongs to the Germanic language family?
questions.explanation: German is a Germanic language, not a Romance language. French, Italian, and Spanish all developed from Latin and are Romance languages derived from Latin.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents that are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. These systems introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation, and reliability compared to single-agent systems. Research work involves open-ended problems where it is very difficult to predict the required steps in advance, making the dynamic nature of multi-agent systems particularly well-suited for these tasks.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system composed of according to the source content?
questions.answer: Multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonContent: Traditional approaches using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) use static retrieval, where they fetch a set of chunks most similar to an input query and use these chunks to generate a response. In contrast, the multi-agent architecture uses a multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers. The Research system creates a LeadResearcher agent that enters an iterative research process, analyzing the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context. This dynamic approach allows the system to adapt as new information is discovered during the research process.
questions.question: Traditional RAG uses static retrieval to fetch chunks most similar to an input query, while the multi-agent Research system uses dynamic multi-step search.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Efficiency in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance, with token usage by itself explaining 80% of the variance. The number of tool calls and model choice were the two other explanatory factors. This validates the architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. However, in practice these architectures burn through tokens fast: agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chats.
questions.question: According to the source content, what percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation is explained by token usage alone?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other factors that together explain 95% of the performance variance.

questions.lessonTitle: Orchestrator Delegation and Task Description Quality
questions.lessonContent: The lead agent in a multi-agent system decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. Early experiments allowed the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage,' but these instructions were vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents. For instance, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains, without an effective division of labor.
questions.question: According to the source content, what problem occurred when the lead agent gave simple, short instructions to subagents?
questions.answer: Subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents, causing duplicated work and gaps in research.

questions.lessonContent: Evaluating multi-agent systems presents unique challenges because agents can take completely different valid paths to reach their goal, even with identical starting points. Traditional evaluations assume the AI follows the same steps each time, but multi-agent systems don't work this way. One agent might search three sources while another searches ten, or they might use different tools to find the same answer. Because developers don't always know what the right steps are, they can't just check if agents followed the 'correct' steps prescribed in advance. Instead, flexible evaluation methods are needed that judge whether agents achieved the right outcomes while also following a reasonable process.
questions.question: Evaluating multi-agent systems is challenging because agents may take different valid paths to reach the same goal, making it impossible to check if they followed prescribed steps in advance.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Based on Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules must be embedded in the prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of the system. The evaluation criteria used by LLM judges include factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.
questions.question: According to the source content, what is the recommended number of subagents and tool calls for complex research tasks?
choices: More than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities, distinguishing it from simple fact-finding (1 agent, 3-10 calls) and direct comparisons (2-4 subagents, 10-15 calls each).

questions.lessonTitle: Agent State Recovery in Production Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means systems need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, restarts are expensive and frustrating for users because they would lose all progress. Instead, Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. They also combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints to handle issues gracefully.
questions.question: What approach did Anthropic build to handle errors in their multi-agent system instead of restarting from the beginning?
questions.answer: Systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred

questions.lessonTitle: Execution Model Limitations in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: The lead agents in Anthropic's Research system execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination because the lead agent knows exactly what state all subagents are in at any moment. However, this design creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents mid-task, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching.
questions.question: The lead agent executes subagents synchronously (waiting for each set to complete before proceeding), which creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents.

questions.lessonTitle: Agent Deployment Strategy for Production Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This creates a deployment challenge: whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their research process. Updating every agent to the new version simultaneously would disrupt ongoing research and lose user progress. To avoid this, Anthropic uses a technique that gradually shifts traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, allowing the system to update without disrupting agents that are mid-process.
questions.question: What technique does Anthropic use to deploy updates to their agent system without disrupting running agents?
choices: Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously
Canary releases that deploy to a small percentage of agents first
Blue-green deployments that instantly switch all agents to the new version
Rolling updates that restart each agent one at a time
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments allow both old and new versions to run simultaneously while gradually shifting traffic, preventing disruption to agents that are mid-process during deployment.

questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent systems, errors can be catastrophic if not handled properly since agents maintain state across long-running processes. When errors occur, the system cannot simply restart from the beginning as this would be expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, the system first notifies the agent of the failure, allowing it to adapt gracefully to the situation. The agent is then able to resume from where it was when the error occurred, leveraging both its intelligence and deterministic safeguards like retry logic to recover and complete the task.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent error recovery workflow?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Embeddings and Together AI Platform
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the platform provides newly released M2-BERT retrieval models designed for long context applications. These M2-BERT models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks. This enables more meaningful contexts to be contained within the embeddings.
questions.question: What are the three available context length options for M2-BERT retrieval models?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Embeddings and Together AI Platform
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI API compatibility to facilitate easy migration for developers. This means if users have already built applications following the OpenAI API, they can easily switch to the Together endpoint by adjusting the base URL to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" and using their Together API key. The compatibility extends to the embeddings create function where input texts and model parameters work similarly to OpenAI's implementation. This feature allows for seamless integration with existing codebases without requiring extensive refactoring.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully OpenAI API compatible, allowing users to migrate by changing the base URL.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Embeddings and Together AI Platform
questions.lessonContent: Together AI positions its embeddings pricing as significantly more competitive than other popular platforms. According to the platform, users can access these powerful embedding models at very competitive prices, achieving up to 4x cost savings compared to alternative platforms. This pricing advantage applies across the range of available models including the state-of-the-art M2-Retrieval models for long context. The combination of high performance (comparable or better accuracies than closed models in MTEB benchmarks) with substantially lower costs makes Together Embeddings an attractive option for developers building AI applications requiring embeddings at scale.
questions.question: Which pricing comparison is explicitly stated in the content about Together Embeddings?
choices: Up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that users can access these powerful models at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides access to various embedding models, including the M2-BERT retrieval models designed for long context applications. One specific model mentioned is M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, which is designed to handle documents up to 8k context length. When working with embedding vectors for visualization or other downstream tasks, knowing the dimensionality of the embedding space is crucial. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model produces embedding vectors with a dimension of 768, which is a standard size for many transformer-based embedding models.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is designed to be OpenAI API compatible, allowing users to easily migrate existing applications. To use the Together API for generating embeddings, developers can use either of two approaches. First, the OpenAI-compatible client requires both an API key and base URL pointing to the Together API endpoint. Second, the native Together client can be initialized by setting the global api_key with `together.api_key = <your-api-key>` and then creating the client with `client = together.Together()`. This native approach does not require a base URL since it uses the default Together endpoint.
questions.question: True or False: The Together API client requires an API key and base URL for initialization.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 open source embedding models, including several that have achieved top positions on the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard. These models have demonstrated comparable or better accuracies than closed commercial models. Among the top models from the MTEB leaderboard mentioned in the content are UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. These models are available alongside the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context applications.
questions.question: Which of the following are mentioned as top models from the MTEB leaderboard available on Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the available models include 'top models from the MTEB leaderboard (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models.' The other options are not mentioned in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: To visualize embeddings, you first need to generate the model embeddings using the Together API with models like M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K. The embedding vectors typically have high dimensions - for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768, which is too large to easily visualize. To plot each data example in 2D, you then transform the embedding vectors using t-SNE. Finally, you can plot the transformed embedding vectors with predefined labels to display the visualization.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to simplify the implementation. The content provides deep-dive tutorials for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768. When plotting each data example in 2D, the code uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional representation suitable for visualization.
questions.question: True or False: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model has an embedding dimension of 768.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example uses sample data from various domains of RedPajama-v1 Sample, including files such as arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, and github_sample.jsonl. After applying tSNE transformation and plotting, the content explicitly states that texts from each data source are somewhat closely located. The visualization also reveals similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are shown to be less related.
questions.question: Based on the visualization results, which pair of data sources showed the closest relationship in the t-SNE plot?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'We can also see the similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are less related.' This directly identifies GitHub and Stackexchange as having the closest relationship in the visualization.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering. The model demonstrates strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. It scores strongly on CursorBench, which is the benchmark of real-world software engineering, while also scoring at frontier levels on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. The model is trained in two phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance.
questions.question: What is Composer 2 designed for?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained in two distinct phases to achieve strong coding performance. The first phase is continued pretraining, which aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding. The second phase is large-scale reinforcement learning, which improves end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch.
questions.question: Composer 2 is trained using a two-phase approach consisting of continued pretraining and reinforcement learning.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves strong performance on multiple evaluation benchmarks. On CursorBench, the internal evaluation suite derived from real software engineering problems, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% accuracy, representing a major improvement over previous Composer models. On public benchmarks, the model scores 73.7% on SWE-bench Multilingual and 61.7% on Terminal-Bench in the Cursor harness, which is comparable to state-of-the-art systems. These scores demonstrate that Composer 2 is competitive with the strongest frontier models.
questions.question: What are the benchmark scores achieved by Composer 2 on CursorBench, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Terminal-Bench respectively?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 61.3 on CursorBench, 73.7 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 61.7 on Terminal-Bench. These are the scores explicitly stated for Composer 2 in the technical report.

questions.lessonContent: The base model selected for Composer 2 is Kimi K2.5, which is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters. This model was chosen after internal evaluations measuring internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking capabilities. The continued pretraining stage extends Kimi K2.5 with a code-dominated data mix and is divided into three phases: the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.
questions.question: What are the total parameter count and active parameter count of the Kimi K2.5 base model used for Composer 2?
questions.answer: 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a highly asynchronous regime for reinforcement learning training with independent training and rollout generation workers. The system maintains stability by minimizing how off-policy the samples become, which is particularly important because agent rollouts can be very long when aiming for long-horizon coherency. On the infrastructure side, this divergence is reduced via fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, similar to PipelineRL. Inference workers are capable of updating weights mid-rollout, which means later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy.
questions.question: In the asynchronous RL training regime for Composer 2, inference workers can update weights mid-rollout. This reduces divergence between the sampling and training policy.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence for regularization during reinforcement learning training. Many open-source implementations estimate KL with the k3 estimator, which is unbiased and reduces variance when policies are close. However, the variance increases drastically as the policies diverge. Therefore, Composer 2 uses the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead of k3, as k1 does not suffer from variance blow-up for large KL values despite being slightly biased.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use to avoid variance blow-up when policies diverge?
questions.explanation: The k1 estimator = -log r is used instead of k3 because k3 suffers from extreme variance increase as policies diverge, while k1 maintains stable estimates even for large KL values.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench was developed to address limitations in public evaluation benchmarks. Unlike public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks compared to 7-10 lines in SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual?

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services that enable larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. These services are: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. Each service can be scaled independently, making training more resilient to failures in individual components.
questions.question: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 is composed of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats for the Mixture-of-Experts layer. For the MoE forward pass, a novel variant of NVFP4 is used where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with a block size of 16 and FP32 per-token scales. For the MoE backward pass, the standard MXFP8 format is used with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. The choice of using different precision formats for forward and backward passes is due to the asymmetry in RL training requirements.
questions.question: Which precision format does Composer 2 use for the MoE backward pass: MXFP8 or NVFP4?
questions.explanation: For the MoE backward pass, Composer 2 uses the standard MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block, while the forward pass uses NVFP4.

questions.lessonContent: When you run the /init command in Claude Code, the tool automatically generates a CLAUDE.md file for you. This special file is pulled into context when starting a conversation, making it an ideal place to document common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, and developer environment setup. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
questions.question: What command automatically generates a CLAUDE.md file for you?

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette like branch naming conventions, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. The content explicitly states there is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, and the recommendation is to keep them concise and human-readable.
questions.question: CLAUDE.md files require a specific format to work properly.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in multiple locations to control when they are pulled into context. The most common usage is placing it at the root of your repo where you run claude from, and it is recommended to name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git so you can share it across sessions and with your team. Alternatively, you can name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. For monorepos, you can place CLAUDE.md files in parent directories of where you run claude, which will be pulled in automatically. You can also place CLAUDE.md files in child directories, and Claude will pull them in on demand when you work with files in those directories.
questions.question: Where can CLAUDE.md files be placed?
choices: Only in the root of your repo and your home folder
Only in the root of your repo
In the root of your repo, parent directories, child directories, or your home folder
Only in parent directories for monorepos
questions.explanation: According to the content, CLAUDE.md files can be placed in four locations: the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

questions.lessonTitle: Exploring, Planning, Coding, and Committing with Claude
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports a flexible workflow called 'Explore, plan, code, commit' that suits many problems.
